ranges.en: Mishna rules that an agent bringing a get from overseas must recite the written-and-signed-in-my-presence formula.
Rabban Gamliel extends the formula to bills brought from the border towns Rekem or Heger.
Rabbi Eliezer extends the formula to the short Ludim-to-Lod route, despite the places being close.
The Rabbis deny the formula is needed, except in the case that follows.
The Rabbis' exception: transfers from overseas to Eretz Yisrael, or between overseas countries, require the formula.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: the formula applies even between districts within the same overseas country.
R. Yehuda fixes the borders: Rekem, Ashkelon and Akko lie outside Eretz Yisrael on their respective sides.
R. Meir holds that Akko counts as Eretz Yisrael for bills of divorce.
Bringing a bill from one place to another within Eretz Yisrael needs no formula.
If the husband contests the bill, it is ratified through its signatories.
The Gemara asks what the reason is for the declaration requirement.
Rabba is named as the one responding; his explanation follows.

ranges.en: Rabba's reason: people overseas are not expert in writing a get for this specific couple.
Rava's rival reason: no witnesses are available to ratify a document written far away.
The Gemara asks what the difference is between the two explanations.
One difference: two bearers of the get, or a transfer within Eretz Yisrael where residents know the requirement.
Another difference: a transfer within the same overseas region, where witnesses are available for Rava's concern.
The Gemara asks why Rabba does not require two witnesses, as for all Torah testimony.
One witness is deemed credible regarding prohibitions, so the requirement is not necessary.
The Gemara objects: perhaps one witness is credible in prohibitions generally, so the principle should apply here.
Example of a doubtful piece of fat where one witness suffices, since no prior prohibition was established.
Here the prohibition is already established, since the woman is a married wife, unlike the fat example.
Principle: matters of sexual impropriety cannot be established by fewer than two witnesses.
Rabba's concern is not mere uncertainty; most people know the rule, even by R. Meir's minority-concern view.
Ordinary judicial scribes who write divorce documents learn this halakha, supporting the defense.
The Sages required testimony as an extra precaution, and the question is applied to this testimony.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis were lenient, out of concern for an agunah, by accepting a single agent's testimony.
The Gemara asks whether this ruling is really a leniency or a stringency.
Requiring two witnesses would bar the husband from contesting, so one agent gives the husband more power to invalidate.
The Gemara cites a teaching about how many people must be present when the get is handed over.
R. Yohanan and R. Hanina dispute whether delivery must be before two or before three people.
The agent takes care at the outset to settle the matter fully, so he does not invalidate his own get.
The Gemara asks why Rava does not require two witnesses, as in ordinary ratification of documents.
One witness is deemed credible regarding prohibitions, so no second witness is needed.
The Gemara objects: perhaps one witness is credible regarding prohibitions generally.
The doubtful fat example shows a single witness suffices where no prior prohibition was established.
Here the woman is presumed forbidden as a married wife, so the fat example does not apply.
Matters of sexual impropriety cannot be established by fewer than two witnesses.
By right, document ratification also should not require two witnesses, following Reish Lakish's view.
Reish Lakish's view: signing witnesses become like witnesses whose testimony was already examined in court.
The Sages nonetheless required the court to ratify documents.
Here the Rabbis were lenient for bills of divorce due to the concern for an agunah.
The Gemara again asks whether the ruling is a leniency or a stringency.
Requiring two witnesses would bar the husband from contesting, so one agent lets him challenge the get.
The Gemara again cites the teaching on how many people must be present at delivery.
R. Yohanan and R. Hanina dispute whether delivery needs two or three people present.
The agent is careful at the outset to settle the matter fully, avoiding an invalid get.
The Gemara asks why Rava does not state the reason as Rabba does, for the woman's sake.
Rava could answer that the mishna does not teach the declaration as 'for her sake'.
Rabba answers that the mishna should teach it so, but the Sages avoided extra wording that could cause error.
The Gemara asks whether the agent will still shorten the formula, as he might with the current wording.
The agent is likely to shorten by omitting one term of three, but not one term of two.
The Gemara asks why Rabba does not say the reason is the availability of witnesses, as Rava does.
Rabba answers that mentioning only signing would suggest the reason is that the get must be written for her sake.
Rava answers that the wording is needed to stop people confusing it with one-witness ratification of other documents.
Rabba responds that the two cases are not comparable, since other documents need only a witness to say they know it.
Further, a woman is credible for a get, and an interested party is credible, unlike with other documents.
Rava challenges Rabba: is it really true that they would not be credible if they only say we know?
Since 'we know' is credible, people would confuse the get with ratification of other documents by one witness.
The Gemara asks, on Rabba's reason, which tanna requires the get to be written for her sake and needs it.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks whether the signing must be done for the woman's sake.
The Gemara proposes that R. Meir requires signing for her sake but not writing for her sake.
A mishna forbids writing on an attached leaf, but a get written that way and then detached and signed is valid.
The Gemara proposes that this mishna follows R. Elazar, who requires writing but not signing for her sake.
The Gemara rejects the claim that the mishna follows R. Elazar, which would conflict with his rule on signing.
The Gemara suggests R. Elazar requires signing for her sake by rabbinic law, not Torah law.
The mishna's three invalid gittin would be valid by Torah law, yet R. Elazar would not require signing for her sake.
A mishna teaches that three defective gittin are invalid ab initio, but offspring of a later marriage are kosher.
The mishna lists three invalid gittin: handwritten without witnesses, undated, and with only one witness.
R. Elazar holds a get delivered before two witnesses is valid even without witnesses' signatures.
Such a get can be collected from liened property, since witnesses sign only for the betterment of the world.
The Gemara proposes the mishna follows R. Meir, who does not require writing for her sake.
The Gemara suggests R. Meir requires writing for her sake by rabbinic law, not Torah law.
Rav Nachman says R. Meir requires no writing for her sake at all, even for a get found in the garbage.

ranges.en: Restates the ruling that a get signed and handed over is valid, as applied to Rav Nachman's garbage case.
If Rav Nachman's ruling were Torah law, he should have said R. Meir requires a Torah-level writing for her sake.
The Gemara retracts and proposes the mishna follows R. Elazar, who does not require signing for her sake.
R. Elazar requires no signing when no witnesses exist, but requires signing for her sake when witnesses are present.
R. Abba reports R. Elazar concedes a get signed by disqualified witnesses is invalid, showing witness signatures must be valid.
Rav Ashi offers another explanation: the mishna follows R. Yehuda, who is the source of the ruling.
A mishna teaches that R. Yehuda invalidates a get unless writing and signing are done on a detached item.
The Gemara asks why we did not simply explain the mishna as following R. Yehuda, whose view is stated in a mishna.
Unattributed mishnayot follow R. Meir, and halakha follows R. Elazar on gittin, so these were tried first.
A mishna teaches that R. Gamliel and R. Eliezer require the declaration for bills brought from border or near areas.
Abaye explains that these are towns near Eretz Yisrael and within its boundary, not part of the land itself.
Rabba bar bar Hana reports from personal observation that Ludim and Lod are a short distance apart.
The Gemara infers that the first tanna holds these residents need not say the declaration.
The Gemara asks whether the two sages are not in fact disputing this underlying principle.
Two reasons: overseas people are not expert in writing for her sake, or witnesses are not available to ratify.
Rejecting the dispute reading: Rabba resolves the mishna's opinions by his own reasoning, and Rava by his.
All agree the reason is that overseas people are not expert in writing for her sake.
The dispute here: the first tanna holds residents near Eretz Yisrael are learned, since they are nearby.
Rabban Gamliel and R. Eliezer each state where residents are learned or not, to exclude distinctions overseas.
Rava reads the same dispute: everyone agrees the reason is lack of witnesses, and nearby towns have them.
Rabban Gamliel and R. Eliezer restate their positions on availability of witnesses in towns near or within the land.
The mishna teaches that the declaration is required only for bringing a get from overseas to Eretz Yisrael or the reverse.
The Gemara infers that the first tanna holds one who delivers a get from Eretz Yisrael overseas need not declare.
The Gemara asks whether the two positions dispute the underlying reason that overseas people are not expert.

ranges.en: The first tanna's reasoning: these travelers are learned, and the reason is that witnesses are not available to ratify.
The Gemara rejects reading the mishna as a dispute: Rabba and Rava each explain it by their own reasoning.
Rabba's view: all agree the reason is lack of expertise, and the dispute concerns a decree on delivering a get.
The first tanna holds the Sages do not decree that one who delivers a get must declare, by analogy to one who brings it.
The later Rabbis hold the Sages decreed the declaration for one who delivers, so the bringer will not err.
Rava reads the dispute as explaining the first tanna's reasoning, since everyone agrees the reason is lack of witnesses.
The mishna teaches that one who brings a get from region to region overseas must make the declaration.
The Gemara infers that within one overseas region the declaration is not required.
This inference works for Rava, but it is difficult for Rabba, since overseas residents are not expert regardless of distance.
Rabba's reply: the inference should instead be that within Eretz Yisrael, region to region, no declaration is needed.
This is objectionable, since the mishna explicitly teaches that bringing a get within Eretz Yisrael needs no declaration.
The explicit teaching would only show it is valid after the fact, so the mishna's ab initio ruling is a needed addition.
Some raise the objection differently, inferring from the mishna that within Eretz Yisrael no declaration is needed.
Reply: the mishna instead teaches that within one overseas region no declaration is needed, not region to region in Eretz Yisrael.
If so, what is the halakha for bringing a get region to region within Eretz Yisrael, and why not state it generally?
Even Rava agrees no declaration is needed within Eretz Yisrael, since pilgrims make witnesses frequently available.
This works only while the Temple stands, so what can be said once it is destroyed?
Fixed central courts exist where everyone goes, so witnesses are frequently available to ratify a get.
The mishna teaches that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires the declaration even between districts of one city.
R. Yitzhak describes the city of Asasiyyot with two governing districts that restricted passage, so the declaration was needed.
Rava's case works, but Rabba must also accept Rava's reason, adding his own reason on expertise.
The Gemara asks what the actual difference is between the explanations of Rava and Rabba.
Alternatively, the difference concerns a transfer within one overseas region, where witnesses are available.
The mishna teaches that if the bearer cannot declare, witness signatures let the get be ratified by its signatories.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'and he is unable to say' means in this halakha.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks whether a deaf-mute can even bring a get, since he is not fit to be an agent.
A mishna teaches that all may bring a get except a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor.
Rav Yosef explains the case: the agent was competent at delivery but became deaf-mute before saying the declaration.
Rav Yosef's explanation works for Rava but is difficult for Rabba, who requires testimony for her sake.
The case refers to later generations, after overseas residents learned the get must be written for her sake.
If the Sages decreed the declaration here too, a deaf-mute should also be disqualified as an agent.
Becoming deaf-mute after competence is uncommon, and the Sages did not decree on uncommon matters.
But a woman bringing her own get is also uncommon, yet the Sages required her to declare.
A mishna teaches that a woman may bring her own get, provided she says the declaration herself.
The Sages decreed this so that agency types are not distinguished, and all agents must declare.
If so, a husband bringing his wife's get should also declare, so why does a baraita exempt him?
A baraita teaches that the husband who brought his own get need not say the declaration.
The decree is because the husband might contest the get, but here he holds it, so the decree does not apply.
Come and hear: Shmuel asked Rav Huna about two people who brought a get from overseas.
Rav Huna rules they need not declare, since two witnesses saying she was divorced are credible anyway.
This works for Rava's witness-based reason, but is difficult for Rabba, who requires written-for-her-sake testimony.
Rabba's case refers to the period after overseas residents learned that the get must be written for her sake.
If so, a single agent should also not need to declare.
One witness still must declare, as a rabbinic decree against the matter returning to its corrupt state.
If so, two people bringing a get should also need to declare, under the same decree.
Two people bringing a get is uncommon, and the Sages did not decree on uncommon matters.
But a woman bringing her own get is also uncommon, and the mishna still requires her declaration.
The mishna teaches that the woman herself may bring her get, but must say the declaration.
This avoids distinguishing agency types, so the agent is not treated differently by category.
If so, the husband who brings his own get should also need to declare.
A baraita teaches that the husband who brings his own get need not say the declaration.
The decree concerns the husband contesting the get, but here he holds it and can simply tear it up.
A tosefta teaches that a get delivered without the declaration is valid if its signatures are ratified.
The tosefta says the declaration was required to be lenient for her, not to be stringent with her.
Rava's reading works, since the declaration avoids ratification. Rabba's reading applies after overseas residents learned the rule.
But the decree that the matter may return to corruption was stated, so why was it not enforced here?
This refers to a woman who married again, and the Gemara says the tosefta's reason is not accurate for that case.
The tanna adds that the declaration was required to be lenient for her, not to be stringent against her new husband.

ranges.en: Asks why the Sages required the agent's declaration at all, if the husband is not contesting the bill.
Introduces the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi over the reason for the declaration.
Infers Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's view from the case of Rabbi Shimon bar Abba bringing him a bill.
Rabbi Shimon bar Abba asks whether he must make the declaration that it was written and signed in his presence.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says no: the declaration was required only in earlier generations, not in later ones.
Objects that this cannot be right, since Rabba holds otherwise and the risk of the matter reverting to corruption remains.
Answers that another person was present with Rabbi Shimon bar Abba, so the two-witness condition was satisfied.
States the dispute over how many witnesses an agent delivering a bill from overseas must have present.
Infers Rabbi Yochanan's view from the case of Ravin bar Rav Chisda, who was told to speak before two witnesses.
Proposes that the two positions rest on different rationales: lack of expertise versus lack of ratifying witnesses.
Rejects that proposal: Rabbi Yochanan would then conflict with the view that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi attributed to him.
Adds that Rabba follows Rava, so even the expertise rationale still requires witnesses to ratify the document.
Resolves that all agree witnesses are needed, and that the dispute concerns whether an agent may serve as witness and judge.
Objects that for rabbinic matters a witness may become a judge, and document ratification is only rabbinic.
Explains that the dispute is instead about women: one Sage fears a woman will bring a bill, the other says people will not rely on her.
Cites a baraita that follows Rabbi Yochanan's two-witness rule, where Rabbi Meir holds the offspring is a mamzer.
Gives the Rabbis' ruling that the offspring is not a mamzer, and the remedy of re-delivering the bill before two witnesses.
Asks whether Rabbi Meir really holds the bill invalid even when the witness saw it written and signed.
Replies yes: Rabbi Meir consistently holds that any deviation from the Sages' bill formula produces a mamzer, citing Rav Hamnuna.
Narrates that bar Haddaya wished to bring a bill from one country to another and asked Rabbi Achai how to proceed.
Rabbi Achai rules that the agent must stand over every letter while the scribe writes the bill.
Bar Haddaya goes to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi to ask whether that close supervision is required.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi reply that it is not required, and that general supervision suffices.
Argues that acting stringently would cast aspersions on earlier bills of divorce, which were not examined so closely.
Rabba bar bar Chana brings a bill half written in his presence and half not, and asks Rabbi Elazar to rule.
Rabbi Elazar rules that even if the scribe wrote one line for her sake before the agent, no further supervision is needed.
Begins Rav Ashi's opinion, which is completed on the next daf.

ranges.en: Teaches that hearing the quill and the scroll being written suffices for the agent's testimony.
Cites a baraita in support of Rav Ashi: an agent may testify even if he and the scribe are in different rooms all day.
Reasons that the baraita must mean the agent heard the writing sounds, since he cannot see the scribe; this supports Rav Ashi.
Quotes the baraita's ruling that a bill entered and exited all day remains valid.
Asks who the one entering and exiting is, and whether the ruling refers to the agent or to the scribe.
Objects that the scribe reading in this way is obvious, since entering and exiting would not invalidate a bill.
Explains the baraita teaches the case of a scribe who leaves for the market, lest someone else commissioned a bill meanwhile.
Records the dispute between Rav and Shmuel on whether Babylonia counts as Eretz Yisrael for bills of divorce.
Proposes that Rav and Shmuel differ on the rationale: lack of expertise for Rav, lack of ratifying witnesses for Shmuel.
Rejects the proposal, since Rabba follows Rava that witnesses are needed to ratify regardless of expertise.
Resolves that all agree on witness ratification, and that Rav and Shmuel differ on whether academy students are available as witnesses.
Cites Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Abba: Babylonia was treated as Eretz Yisrael for divorce from Rav's arrival.
Raises an objection from a Mishnah and a verse placing Babylonia north of Eretz Yisrael, hence outside its bill rules.
Resolves the objection: Rabbi Meir's rule that Akko counts as Eretz Yisrael applies only to nearby Akko, not distant Babylonia.
Asks where the boundaries of Babylonia lie for the purpose of bills of divorce.
Presents Rav Pappa's view that the bills dispute mirrors the lineage dispute, against Rav Yosef, who limits it to lineage.
Reports Rav Chisda's ruling on which bills from Akteisfon and Bei Ardeshir require the agent's declaration.
Proposes that Rav Chisda holds the expertise rationale, since Bei Ardeshir residents are learned in writing bills.
Rejects the proposal: Rabba follows Rava, so witnesses must ratify the document in every case.
Upholds Rav Chisda: Akteisfon residents recognize the signatures of Bei Ardeshir residents, who frequent their market.
Asks why the Bei Ardeshir residents do not recognize the signatures of the Akteisfon residents.
Replies that the Bei Ardeshir residents are preoccupied with their market business and so do not learn the signatures.
Reports graded requirements: Rabba bar Avuh, Rav Sheshet and Rava each require the declaration for progressively closer transfers.
Asks why Rava requires the declaration even within one house group, given that he holds the witness rationale.
Explains Rava decreed this only for Meḥoza, whose residents move often, so witnesses may have left town.
Rav Ḥanin relates that Rav Kahana brought a bill of divorce of uncertain direction and came before Rav.
Rav Kahana asks Rav whether he must state the declaration that it was written and signed in his presence.
Rav replies that Rav Kahana is not required to make the declaration.

ranges.en: Restates the principle that acting in this way brings benefit to the bill of divorce.
Asks what is meant by the claim that acting in this way brings benefit.
Explains that the husband's later contest is disregarded, so the bill cannot be challenged.
Brings a Tosefta case where Rabbi Yishmael requires the agent to make the declaration, so witnesses are not needed later.
Rabbi Elai objects that Sisai lies within Eretz Yisrael and is close, so Rabbi Meir's Akko rule should apply there too.
Rabbi Yishmael upholds his ruling: since the divorce was issued permissibly, it stands and cannot later be contested.
Asks why Rabbi Yishmael needed to explain his reasoning to Rabbi Elai, since he had already stated it.
Replies that the bystanders had not finished relaying Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning to Rabbi Elai.
Reports Rabbi Evyatar's letter exempting Babylonian bills from the declaration, and proposes the rationale behind it.
Challenges that proposal: Rabba and Rava require ratifying witnesses, and many travelers make witnesses available.
Rav Yosef doubts Rabbi Evyatar's reliability, noting he wrote to Rav Yehuda with a questionable remark.
Quotes the verse Rabbi Evyatar cited to Rav Yehuda, and notes he wrote it without scoring the parchment.
Rabbi Yitzchak rules how many words may be written without scoring the parchment, and a baraita sets the limit at three.
Abaye defends Rabbi Evyatar: a tradition may be unknown to someone, unlike a matter of reasoning.
Adds that God agreed with Rabbi Evyatar's reading of the Gibeah concubine verse in Judges 19:2.
Presents the two explanations of the concubine episode: Rabbi Evyatar's fly versus Rabbi Yonatan's hair.
Narrates Rabbi Evyatar encountering Elijah and asking him what God is doing.
Rabbi Evyatar asks Elijah what the Holy One, Blessed be He, is doing now.
Elijah replies that God is studying the episode of the concubine in Gibeah.
Rabbi Evyatar asks what God says about the episode.
Elijah reports God's words: Evyatar, My son, says this and Yonatan, My son, says that.
Rabbi Evyatar objects: God forbid, is there uncertainty before Heaven, and why cite both opinions?
Elijah replies both are words of the living God, describing how the fly and the hair each provoked a different response.
Rav Yehuda offers a different explanation: the fly was an accident, while the hair was due to her negligence and was dangerous.
Rav Chisda teaches that one must not impose excessive fear on one's household, citing the concubine of Gibeah.
Rav Yehuda, in the name of Rav, lists three sins that result from imposing excessive fear in one's home.
Rabba bar bar Chana adds that on Shabbat eve a person must ask his household three questions before lighting the lamp.

ranges.en: Advises saying instructions calmly so they are accepted, and reports Rav Ashi applying Rabba bar bar Chana's teaching through his own reasoning.
Rabbi Abbahu teaches that one must never impose excessive fear on one's household, citing a great man who was nearly fed forbidden food.
Asks who that individual was, then challenges whether they actually fed him forbidden food, since God would not cause such an error.
Explains they only sought to feed him forbidden food, a limb cut from a living animal, which nearly happened.
Mar Ukva asks Rabbi Elazar whether he may hand over his tormentors to the government when he has the power to do so.
Rabbi Elazar replies with Psalms 39:2: he will keep silent with his mouth even while the wicked stand before him.
Mar Ukva reports that the tormentors are troubling him greatly and he cannot endure them.
Rabbi Elazar advises patient silence, citing Psalms 37:7, predicting the tormentors will fall away on their own.
Reports that Geneiva, Mar Ukva's tormentor, was placed in a neck iron as a result of Rabbi Elazar's advice.
Mar Ukva's associates ask from where song is derived as forbidden in the present era after the Temple's destruction.
Mar Ukva replies by scoring the parchment and citing Hosea 9:1: do not rejoice, Israel, as the nations do.
Asks why he did not reply with Isaiah 24:9, which would show that song is no longer allowed.
Explains a verse about song would be read as limited to instruments, so Mar Ukva taught that all song is forbidden.
Rav Huna bar Natan asks Rav Ashi the meaning of the cities listed in Joshua 15:22.
Rav Ashi replies that the verse is simply listing cities of Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Huna rejects that answer: he knows the verse lists cities, but a deeper reading is intended.
Presents Rav Geviha of Argiza's homiletic reading: the jealous person who stays silent is judged by the Eternal One.
Rav Ashi challenges the method: apply the same reading to Ziklag, Madmannah and Sansannah in Joshua 15:31.
Rav Huna answers that Rav Geviha, if present, would supply an explanation for that verse too.
Rav Aha of Bei Choza'a offers his own reading: one with a complaint over a sip, silent, is judged by the one in the burning bush.
The Exilarch asks Rav Huna from where the prohibition on placing a garland on a groom's head derives.
Rav Huna replies that it is rabbinic, decreed in Vespasian's war, as taught in a mishna in Sota.
Narrates that Rav Huna stepped away, and Rav Chisda then spoke up to the Exilarch.
Rav Chisda cites Ezekiel 21:31, the mitre removed and the garland taken off, as a verse supporting the decree.
Asks how a mitre can be connected to a garland, since they are not worn by the same kind of person.
Explains the verse means that while the mitre is on the High Priest's head, every bridegroom wears a garland, and when it is removed, so is the garland.
Rav Huna returns and rules that the prohibition is rabbinic, while praising Rav Chisda for finding a fine source.
Narrates Ravina finding Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a garland for his daughter at her wedding.
Ravina asks whether Mar does not hold the halakha derived from the mitre and garland verse.
Mar replies the prohibition applies to men, who resemble the High Priest, and not to women.
Asks what the expression this shall no more be the same means in the verse.
Rabbi Avira reads the verse homiletically, transmitting it in the names of Rav Ami and Rav Asi.
The ministering angels object that Israel, who said we will do before we will hear, should not be treated thus.
God replies that Israel deserves this, since they lowered the exalted and set up an idol in the Sanctuary.
Rabbi Avira reads a verse in Nahum homiletically: one should give charity from limited means, all the more so from abundance.
Asks what the phrase even so shall they be cut down, and the phrase nagozzu, means in the verse.
A Sage from the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that one who shears some property for charity is saved from Gehenna.
Offers a parable of two sheep crossing water, one shorn and one not, to illustrate the teaching about charity and Gehenna.

ranges.en: Cites the rest of Nahum 1:12, which speaks of afflicting and then not afflicting again, as the basis for the charity teaching.
Mar Zutra teaches that even a poor man sustained by charity must give charity, and Rav Yosef teaches that God stops showing signs of poverty.
Quotes the mishna in which Rabbi Yehuda sets the boundaries of Eretz Yisrael, with Akko on its northern edge.
Asks whether the mishna means that Akko lies to the north of Eretz Yisrael.
Raises a contradiction from a baraita: the road from Akko to Keziv and beyond shows Akko is not the northern border.
Abaye replies that a strip extends northward from Akko and remains part of Eretz Yisrael, though the general border is at Akko.
Answers that a tanna can indeed mark an area this narrow, as a verse marks a road as a sign.
Cites Judges 21:19 on Shiloh by the east side of the highway, and Rav Pappa explains it as east of the road.
Presents a baraita: one who brings a bill written on a boat in Eretz Yisrael is treated as bringing it within Eretz Yisrael.
Presents a second baraita that treats a bill written on a boat in Eretz Yisrael as if brought from outside the land.
Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction: one baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, the other the Rabbis, as a mishna in Chalah shows.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the boat's soil counts as Eretz Yisrael only when the boat skims the sea floor.
Abaye reconciles both baraitot as following Rabbi Yehuda, distinguishing a boat that skims the sea floor from one that does not.
Rabbi Zeira applies the boat dispute to a perforated flowerpot resting on pegs, placing it within the same disagreement.
Rava objects that Rabbi Yehuda may hold his view only for a boat, so the application to a flowerpot fails.

ranges.en: Distinguishes a boat, which moves, from a flowerpot, which stays fixed, and suggests airspace separates the flowerpot soil from the ground.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds the dispute concerns only the Great Sea, since rivers in the land clearly count as Eretz Yisrael.
Cites a Tosefta on the borders of Eretz Yisrael, drawing a line from Turei Amnon to the River of Egypt, with islands on each side.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that anything directly across from Eretz Yisrael, including the sea, counts as part of it, citing Numbers 34:6.
Asks what the Rabbis do with the verse saying and for the border, which seems to support Rabbi Yehuda.
Replies that the verse teaches that the islands count as Eretz Yisrael, while Rabbi Yehuda says islands need no verse.
Quotes the mishna in which Rabbi Meir holds that Akko is like Eretz Yisrael for bills of divorce.
Sages pose a dilemma to Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba: is selling a slave to a master in Syria like selling outside the land?

Baraita: a slave who brings a manumission document saying you and my property are yours frees himself but not the property.
Dilemma: if the document says all my property is transferred to you, what is the halakha?
Abaye holds that since he acquires himself, he thereby acquires the property as well.
Rava objects: freedom can be granted like a get, but the property transfer is like an unratified document and fails.
Abaye reverses himself: since he does not acquire the property, he does not acquire himself either.

Baraita showing how Rabbi Yosei praised the Sages' words, citing a verse about giving right answers, while the halakha still follows Rabbi Meir.

ranges.en: Baraita: documents from gentile courts are valid except divorce and manumission; Rabbi Meir adds a fourth shared rule, the right to retract the instruction.

Tests each possible tanna as the mishna's author, asking what each view implies for Samaritan testimony on other documents and on divorce bills.

ranges.en: Explains that the Jew would sign alongside a Samaritan only if he were a ḥaver, which is why the mishna's ruling applies to him.

Reply: a Jew signing last does not prove the Samaritan was a ḥaver, since he may have left space above for an elder.

Mishna: documents from gentile courts are valid despite gentile signatures, except divorce and manumission; Rabbi Shimon says these are valid too.

Shmuel: the law of the kingdom is law, so any property transfer accepted by local law is valid in halakha as well.

Mishna: Rabbi Shimon holds that even bills of divorce and manumission are valid when written and signed by gentiles.

ranges.en: Resolution: the case concerns unambiguous gentile names, so no one would rely on those signers as witnesses to the transfer.

Ravina holds that a document written by a group of gentiles should be valid.
Objection from Rafram: the mishna validates gentile-court documents only when produced in an important court, not by any group of gentiles.
Rava rules that a Persian document transferred before Jewish witnesses allows collection from unencumbered property, though not from all sold land.

Answer: Rava refers to witnesses who know how to read Persian.
Objection: a valid document must be written so it cannot be forged, and Persian documents do not meet this standard.
Answer: Rava's ruling applies where the paper was treated with gall, making forgery of the writing impossible.
Objection: a valid document must restate its essential topic in its final line, which Persian documents lack.
Answer: Rava's ruling applies where the document does restate its essential topic in the final line.
Asks why, if the document equals a Jewish one, Rava does not allow collection from liened property as well.
Answer: the document creates no publicity among Jews, so like an oral loan, collection is limited to unencumbered property.
Reish Lakish poses a dilemma to Rabbi Yoḥanan, which the daf leaves unfinished at its end.

Mishna: if the giver of a divorce or manumission instruction wishes to retract before delivery, he may retract, according to Rabbi Meir.

Narrative: Rav Huna, while Rabbi Yirmeya dozed, infers from the Rabbis' ruling that a seizure on a creditor's behalf acquires for him.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef asks whether this holds even when the seizure harms other creditors; Rav Huna answers yes.

Mishna on pe'a: one who gathers produce for a named poor man; Rabbi Eliezer says it is acquired for him, while the Sages give it to the first poor person.

ranges.en: Objection to Rav Hisda's conclusion: perhaps Rabbi Eliezer's view applies only where the collector could have acquired the pe'a for himself.

Inference from the mishna: a master may tell his slave to work for him while he withholds sustenance.

Asks why the mishna allows a husband to say the same to his wife, given that the mishna treats wives differently from slaves.
Reply: the mishna's wife is one whose earnings do not suffice for her sustenance, and then the husband cannot stipulate this.
Objection: the slave case then also concerns one whose earnings do not suffice, so the master may refuse sustenance and the proof stands.
Reply: a slave whose work is not worth his bread is of no use to his master, so the mishna cannot refer to such a case.
Baraita: a slave exiled to a city of refuge is not sustained by his master, and his earnings there belong to the master.
Inference: a master may tell his slave to work for him while he withholds sustenance.
Reply: the baraita refers to a master who told the slave to spend his earnings on his own sustenance.
Asks why the earnings belong to the master if he was told to sustain himself; surplus should obviously belong to the master.
Reply: the ruling is needed, lest one think that since the master does not feed a slave who earns little, he should not take the surplus.
Asks what distinguishes the slave exiled to a city of refuge, since surplus should belong to the master wherever he is.
Reply: one might think the verse on exile to refuge cities gives the exiled slave extra life, so the baraita rules that no such allowance applies.

Asks the purpose of this halakha about the exiled woman, since the same rule applies to all wives whose earnings suffice.

Suggests a tannaitic dispute: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel lets a slave demand sustenance or freedom in famine; the Rabbis leave it to the master.
Proposed reading: the Rabbis and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagree on whether a master may stop sustaining a working slave.
Rejects this reading: the baraita's wording would then be inaccurate, and famine years should not differ from other years.
Reply: the baraita concerns a master who said spend your earnings, and famine prices leave the slave unable to support himself.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: the slave may demand freedom or sustenance so that people see his plight and pity him.
Rabbis: freedom is unnecessary for charity, since those who pity free people also pity a slave, so the baraita does not address the master's right.
Proof from Rav: when a master consecrates his slave's labor, the slave borrows to eat and repays later, suggesting the master need not sustain him.
Reply: the case is one where the master does provide sustenance.
Asks what the point is, if the master provides sustenance in any case.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks whether the slave borrows and eats for surplus food when his master already provides for him.

Consecration is preferable for the treasury itself, since a stronger slave who eats extra food is worth more.
Restates the halakha that the slave borrows, eats, works, and repays the loan.
Objection: the slave's work is consecrated, so how can he use it to repay a loan?
Resolution: he earns only amounts below one peruta, which are not consecrated, so he can repay in small sums.
It is reasonable to read Rav's ruling as referring to a case where the master provides sustenance.
Rav's ruling that a consecrated slave works and eats, since otherwise no one would work to support him.
If the earlier halakha concerns a master who sustains the slave, the two statements of Rav do not contradict each other.
If the first halakha also covers a master who does not sustain him, the reasoning about who will work for him fails.
Must one conclude that Rav holds a master cannot tell his slave to work without being sustained?
Yes, one concludes that the master cannot say to the slave: work for me but I will not sustain you.

With what case are we dealing here?
It deals with a case where the master provides the slave's sustenance.
If so, why does the slave live on charity when he already has sustenance from his master?

Difficulty: if so, the phrase that he is sustained from charity is imprecise; it should say he earns a living.
Must one conclude from this wording that Rabbi Yochanan holds the master can say work for me but I will not sustain you?
Indeed, one concludes that this is the case.
The Mishnah states that the master receives compensation for the slave's lost livelihood and medical costs.
Explanation: the loss of livelihood is obvious, so the Mishnah needed to specify only the medical costs.
Difficulty: the medical-cost compensation should belong to the slave, since he needs it to be healed.
No, it is needed for a case where doctors estimated five days of healing but a strong medicine healed him in three.
Lest one say the pain the slave endured from the strong medicine was his, so the money should belong to him.
Rabbi Yochanan teaches that even this money belongs to the master, not the slave.
A baraita introduces Rabbi Elazar's report of the exchange with Rabbi Meir.
Objection to Meir: emancipation is surely a benefit to the slave, since it frees him from his master.
Meir replies that it is a detriment: if the slave were a priest's, emancipation would disqualify him from teruma.
Objection: if the master may refuse to sustain him, the slave has no guaranteed sustenance to lose on emancipation.
Meir's proof: a priest's fleeing slave or rebellious wife still eats teruma, but an emancipated slave may not.
Conclusion: a bill of divorce is to a wife's detriment, since it disqualifies her from teruma and cuts off her maintenance.
What did the Rabbis say to Meir, and how did he respond to them?
Meir's reply: you answered me about sustenance; what will you answer me about teruma?
Objection: if the master wishes, he can throw the emancipation document near the slave and disqualify him from teruma.
The slave can avoid this by leaving his master, escaping, and going out into the world.

ranges.en: Meir's argument: a priest's fleeing slave or rebellious wife still eats teruma, but an emancipated slave may not, so emancipation harms him.

Mishnah: a bill of divorce or manumission cannot be delivered after the husband or master dies, but a sum of money may be given after death.

Rav Pappa: the mishnah deals with a dying person, following another ruling of Rav.

From where does one know this?
The mishnah: one who says to give a bill of divorce or manumission and then dies, the document is not given after death.
Inference: the ruling concerns a dead man, and a dying person who did not say give still has the document delivered.
A mishnah: one led out to execution who says to write a divorce for his wife, the document is written and given even without the word give.
Rabbi Shimon Shezuri includes a dangerously ill person, so a dying person need only say write.
Rav Ashi objects: why assume the mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rather than the Rabbis, who would allow a dying person's case?
Rav Huna cites Rav: a sum placed in the presence of all three parties is acquired by the recipient.
Rava: Rav's rule stands to reason only for deposits, where specific money is transferred, not for loans.
Rava swears that Rav in fact stated the rule for loans as well.
Shmuel in the name of Levi: the same acquisition applies to a loan that the debtor owes, if done in the presence of all three.

Ameimar: it becomes like a borrower telling the lender, when the loan is given, that he is obligated to the lender and to whoever comes on his authority.
Rav Ashi objects: then a transfer to people not yet born at the time of the loan should also fail to be acquired.

Rav Ashi states the final reason for the matter.

ranges.en: Explains the benefit a borrower gains when his debt passes to a new lender, since he can seek an extension from that lender.

Mar Zutra's teaching: three rulings the Sages instituted as halakha without any stated reason.
Examples of such rulings: a gift of all property to a wife makes her only a steward, and a house given at a son's wedding becomes his.
Rav's case: he tells Rav Aha Bardela to pay a sum to a third party, saying it in his presence so that he cannot retract.
Can one infer that the giver could have retracted if he had not stated it in the presence of the recipient?
Rav was not adding a condition; statements made in the presence of all three parties cannot be retracted.
Why is this statement of Rav recorded at all, since Rav already stated the halakha once?
Rav Huna cites Rav: a sum placed with a third party in the presence of all three parties is acquired by that third party.
Had the rule derived only from that case, it would apply only to large gifts; Rav teaches it applies in all cases.
Gardeners settle accounts; one owes an extra sum to the landowner, who acquires it in the presence of the landowner. The gardener later recalculates and brings the matter before Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman: the landowner acquired the money by Rav Huna's rule, and the gardener also performed an actual act of acquisition.
Rava asks whether the gardener refused to pay at all, or merely claimed the money was not in his possession, which would bear on acquisition.
Rav Nachman replies: then it is an acquisition made in error, and any acquisition made in error reverts to the previous owner.
Dilemma: a sender tells an agent to deliver money he owes to someone; can the sender retract after paying the agent?
Rav's view: the sender bears responsibility for the loss, so he cannot retract once the money is delivered.
Shmuel's view: because the sender bears responsibility, the money remains in his domain, so he can retract.
The Gemara suggests the amoraim disagree over whether saying deliver equals saying acquire.

A baraita following Rav: when the sender pays on behalf of a debt or a deposit, he bears responsibility for the loss and cannot retract.

Rabbi Zeira: this refers to a sender who is established as a denier of obligations, so the owner prefers the transfer.
Rav Sheshet had a credit of cloaks in Mehoza; Rav Yosef brought him the money, and the merchants asked him to make an acquisition, which he declined.

ranges.en: Rabbi Ahai sends agents to fetch the vessel; its holders ask for an acquisition to bind the agents, who refuse and return it.

Concludes the halakha refers to a bound slave, who cannot move and so is not treated as a mobile courtyard.
Rava rules that a bill of divorce placed in a courtyard, with a gift deed of that courtyard, divorces her immediately.
Explains why Rava needed to teach both the slave and courtyard cases, so that a decree applied to one would not be extended to the other.
Abaye challenges Rava: a courtyard acquires for her like her hand, even against her will, but a gift needs consent, so the cases differ.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects: agency for receiving a divorce works only with her consent, yet an agent still serves, so the analogy breaks.
Abaye answers that agency comes from a separate verse, and adds that a father can receive a divorce for his minor daughter against her will.
Quotes the mishna: a bill of divorce may be written on an olive leaf, a cow's horn, or a slave's hand, if the husband gives the slave or cow.
Opens a question about the mishna's cases, beginning with why the slave's hand is acceptable.

ranges.en: Asks why the mishna requires giving the whole cow, when the horn alone could be cut off and handed over.
The verse excludes an item lacking writing, cutting, and giving, so a horn alone is invalid and the whole cow must be given.
Mishna: R. Yosei HaGelili says a bill of divorce may not be written on something living or on food.
Asks the basis of R. Yosei HaGelili's view, as a baraita teaches it.
A baraita derives from the word scroll that a bill must be written on something neither living nor food, like a scroll.
Asks how the Rabbis read the word sefer, if it teaches that the bill must contain a proper account of the matters.
Asks what the Rabbis do with the phrase 'and he writes her'.
For the Rabbis the phrase teaches that divorce requires writing and not money, unlike betrothal, which may be effected by money.
Asks how R. Yosei HaGelili derives his reasoning from the verse.
The phrase scroll of severance shows that only a written document severs the marriage, and nothing else does.
Asks what the Rabbis do with the phrase a thing that severs between him and her.
A baraita: a divorce conditioned permanently on not drinking wine or visiting her father's house does not sever; a thirty-day condition does.
Asks how R. Yosei derives from the expanded term keritut that a permanent condition invalidates the divorce.
The Rabbis derive nothing from the expansion of karet to keritut.
Mishna: one may not write on something attached to the ground; if written attached, then detached and signed, it is valid. R. Yehuda disagrees.
Mishna: R. Yehuda ben Beteira forbids erased paper and unfinished leather because they can be forged; the Sages validate such a bill.
Asks why the mishna's first clause forbids writing on attached items if a later clause permits it.
Rav Yehuda, Shmuel and others say the mishna applies when a place was left blank for the essential part, written after detaching.
Holds that the mishna follows R. Elazar, for whom delivery before witnesses effects the divorce, so the restriction covers the essential writing.
Explains the mishna: the standard part may not be written on attached items lest the essential part be written, but detached writing is valid.
Reish Lakish offers a different reading: the mishna refers to signing by witnesses, following R. Meir, so the restriction applies to signing.
A bill written on the clay of a perforated plant pot is valid, since one can take the pot and give it to her.
Asks the halakha for a bill written on a leaf of a plant growing in a perforated pot.
Abaye rules that such a bill written on a leaf is valid.
Rava rules that such a bill written on a leaf is invalid.
Abaye restates his view that the bill is valid.

ranges.en: Continues Abaye's rationale: he can lift the pot with the leaf inside and hand it to her.
Rava holds the bill invalid, due to a decree lest one cut off the leaf and give it to her separately.
Case of a pot owned by one person and plants owned by another, and how each sale is acquired by pulling or taking possession.
Cites the mishna in Kiddushin: movable property is acquired with land-like property through money, a document, or taking possession.
Explains that taking only the pot does not acquire it; the pot is acquired only once the plants are taken into possession.
Poses the case of a perforated pot on the border, with roots in Eretz Yisrael and branches outside, for its tithe status.
Abaye holds we follow the perforation, so the plant counts as growing in Eretz Yisrael.
Rava holds we follow the branches, so the plant counts as growing outside Eretz Yisrael.
Clarifies the dispute: where the roots have taken hold all agree, and the disagreement concerns only unrooted plants.
Challenges with a mishna on adjacent gardens where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree about vegetables growing between them.
Explains R. Meir's reasoning: the upper owner could remove the earth, so his ability to destroy the plants shows ownership.
Explains R. Yehuda's reasoning: the lower owner could fill his airspace with earth, so his control shows ownership.
Challenges that the roots-based disagreement appears in a baraita on a tree partly in and partly out of Eretz Yisrael.
Asks whether the baraita concerns branches in and out of the land while the roots are in one location.
Rejects this reading: the case has roots both inside and outside the land.
Asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning is, since the source of each fruit cannot be determined.
A rock divides the roots up to the trunk, so the parts drawing from each land can be distinguished.
Asks the reasoning of R. Yehuda HaNasi, and what principle the two Sages actually disagree about.
One Sage holds the air mixes the nutrients; the other holds each part stands alone, as if the tree were cut along the border.
Restates the mishna: R. Yehuda ben Beteira bars bills on forgeable surfaces, while the Sages validate them.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ami, in Ulla's name, says there are three hides: matza, ḥifa, and diftera.
Matza is a plain hide, not salted, not floured, and not treated with gallnuts.
Asks which halakha concerns this hide and what its measure is for carrying out on Shabbat.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda says the measure is enough to wrap a small weight.
Asks how large that small weight is.
Abaye answers: a quarter of a quarter of a litra by the Pumbedita weight standard.
Ḥifa is salted but not floured and not treated with gallnuts.
Asks which halakha concerns ḥifa and what its measure is for carrying out on Shabbat.
Cites a mishna: the measure for carrying out a hide is enough to make an amulet.
Diftera is salted and floured, but not treated with gallnuts.
Asks which halakha concerns diftera.
Asks what its measure is.
Its measure is enough to write a bill of divorce on it.
Mishna: the Sages validate bills of divorce written on such surfaces.
Asks who the Sages in the mishna are.
The amora R. Elazar introduces his answer, identifying the Sages in question.

ranges.en: The tanna R. Elazar holds that witnesses to the transmission of a bill of divorce effect the divorce.
The amora R. Elazar limits that view to immediate testimony, since later testimony risks an undetected erased stipulation.
R. Yoḥanan holds even testimony up to ten days later is valid, since witnesses would remember any stipulation.
The amora R. Elazar says the tanna's view covers only bills of divorce, not other documents.
Cites Jeremiah 32:14, that documents be kept in a vessel so they last many days, to show other documents must be durable.
R. Yoḥanan holds that the tanna's view extends even to other documents.
Objects that the verse in Jeremiah says the documents should remain many days, which would seem to require durability.
That verse gives good advice rather than a halakhic requirement, advising durable writing for ownership proof.
Mishna: anyone may write a bill of divorce, including a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, and a woman may write her own, with the writer's receipt also valid.
Asks how a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor can write a bill of divorce, since they lack halakhic competence.
Introduces Rav Huna's reply to the question.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the principle: the bill is valid only when an adult stands over the writer and instructs him to write it for her sake.
Rav Nahman challenges: if a supervising adult validates a disqualified writer, a gentile under a Jew's supervision should too, yet a baraita disqualifies gentiles.
Rav Huna replies that a gentile acts on his own intention, while the mishna's writers lack competence and follow the supervisor.
Rav Nahman retracts: the mishna's disqualification of gentile agents implies by inference that a gentile is qualified to write.
Asks how this fits with a baraita that disqualifies a gentile from writing a bill of divorce.
That baraita follows R. Elazar, who requires writing for her sake, and a gentile acts on his own will and cannot be supervised.
Rav Nahman cites R. Meir: a bill found in a refuse heap, signed by witnesses and given to her, is valid if written for her sake.
Rava objects: the verse and he writes her means the actual writing must be for her sake, not the signatures.
No, the verse refers to the witnesses' signing, which is what must be done for her sake.
Rava objects with a mishna: a bill not written for a specific woman is invalid.
Rav Nahman answers that the mishna means a bill not signed for a specific woman is invalid.
Rava objects with a baraita: writing the essential part for her sake makes the whole bill count as written for her sake.
Rav Nahman rejects this: the baraita concerns signing for her sake, and these sources follow R. Elazar's view that delivery effects divorce.
Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name, and Rabbi Hagga in Ulla's name, hold the mishna applies only when the essential part was left for a competent writer.
R. Zeriqa in R. Yoḥanan's name: writing for her sake is not Torah law; only signing for her sake matters, following R. Meir.
Asks: didn't Rabba bar bar Ḥana say R. Yoḥanan follows R. Elazar, so how can R. Abba say he follows R. Meir?
The Amoraim disagree about R. Yoḥanan's position, whether he explains the mishna by R. Meir or by R. Elazar.
Mishna: anyone may bring a bill except a deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, blind person, or gentile; competence at start and end decides fitness.
Asks why a blind person is disqualified too, since the others lack competence and gentiles are not bound by such laws.
Rav Sheshet: a blind agent cannot know from whom he takes the bill or to whom he gives it, so he cannot testify.
Rav Yosef objects: a blind husband has relations with his wife, and people recognize each other in the dark by voice, so the reason fails.
Rav Yosef answers that the case is outside Eretz Yisrael, where the agent must testify it was written and signed in his presence.
Abaye objects: one who became blind after seeing the writing would then be fit too, yet the mishna requires recovered sight.
The Gemara replies: a blind agent may still testify, and the mishna mentions recovered sight only by parallel with the mental-competence case.
Rav Ashi argues the mishna's wording precisely requires competence at both beginning and end, not merely fitness, which bears on the blind agent.
They asked R. Ami whether a slave may be made an agent to receive a woman's bill of divorce from her husband's hand.
R. Ami begins to answer from the mishna's explicit disqualification of a gentile, by inference about a slave.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes by inference that a slave is fit to serve as an agent.
R. Asi, in R. Yoḥanan's name: a slave cannot receive a divorce from her husband's hand, since he is not included in divorce and betrothal laws.
R. Elazar objects: if the reason is that a slave is outside the matter, then in matters where he is included he should be fit.
Objects with teruma mishnayot: a gentile's or Samaritan's separation of teruma from their own produce counts, yet a gentile agent's separation for a Jew does not.
Asks the reason a gentile agent is disqualified in the teruma mishna.
Numbers 18:28 'so you also' is expounded to mean agents must be Jews, like those appointing them, which excludes slaves.
The school of R. Yannai reads 'so you also' as requiring agents to be members of the covenant, which slaves are, so slaves may act where included.
R. Ḥiyya bar Abba, in R. Yoḥanan's name, repeats that a slave cannot receive a divorce from her husband's hand.
Objects with a mishna: a pregnant slave's unborn child is freed by the master's words, suggesting a slave can acquire for another.
Asks how the clause about a pregnant slave acquiring freedom connects to R. Yoḥanan's statement.
Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda reports R. Yoḥanan's two statements: a slave may receive a bill for a fellow slave from the fellow's master, but not from his own.
If questioned, reply that two sages, R. Zeira and R. Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak, already explained the matter.
One explains it as R. Yehuda HaNasi's view that freeing half a slave frees half; the other says a fetus is part of the mother's body.
Mishna: women not credible to say a husband died may still bring her bill of divorce, since she states it was written and signed before her.
A baraita says just as these women cannot testify that a husband died, they cannot bring her bill of divorce, contradicting the mishna.
Rav Yosef: no difficulty; the mishna is in Eretz Yisrael, where she only acts as agent, while the baraita outside it relies on her statement.
Abaye reverses the distinction: in Eretz Yisrael her bill is not credible, since a husband's challenge matters; outside, it is credible.
A baraita supports Abaye: R. Shimon ben Elazar, in R. Akiva's name, infers a fortiori that a woman may bring her own bill of divorce.

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Infers from the baraita's wording that a wife bringing a bill from outside Eretz Yisrael must also state it was written and signed before her.
Rav Ashi: the mishna's precise wording, that the woman herself must state it was written and signed before her, supports Abaye's view.
Asks, according to Rav Yosef, whether the mishna's first and last clauses concern outside Eretz Yisrael while the middle concerns inside.
Yes: the first and last clauses concern outside Eretz Yisrael, and the middle clause concerns Eretz Yisrael.
Explains the inference: the mishna says only the writing proves the divorce, so her statement is unneeded, indicating the case is in Eretz Yisrael.
The mishna teaches that the woman herself may bring her own bill and must state it was written and signed in her presence.
Asks whether, once the bill reaches her hand, she is divorced automatically.
Rav Huna: the mishna concerns a husband who says she is divorced only before a particular court.
Asks why she must bring the bill and testify, since once she reaches that court she is divorced by it.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika: the husband told her to place the bill on the ground upon arrival and take it, so divorce is not immediate.
Challenges: this resembles a husband telling his wife to take the bill from the ground, which Rava holds counts as nothing.
Alternatively, the husband made her his agent for delivery until arrival, then agent for receipt, so she receives the bill as agent.
Challenges: her delivery agency has not returned to the husband, so the appointment is deficient and the divorce fails.
Asks how this works for the view that a woman may appoint an agent to receive from her husband's agent, and what for the view that she may not.
The view barring such agency rests on the husband's degradation, which he does not mind here because he instructed her.
Asks what can be said if the reason is instead a decree concerning a courtyard that comes afterward.
On the courtyard view, the mishna means she is delivery agent until arrival, then appoints another delivery agent and receives from him.
Alternatively: she is delivery agent until arrival, then says before the court it was written and signed in her presence, and the court appoints her agent.
Chapter-closing formula, Hadran Alakh HaMevi Get, marking the end of the chapter.
Mishna: a bill not written for a specific woman is invalid, illustrated by a man who overhears scribes dictating another man's divorce with his name.
Mishna continues: a bill written for one man's divorce, if reconsidered and used by a townsman with the same names, is invalid for the second man.

ranges.en: Mishnah opening: a man with two same-named wives who wrote a divorce for the older one and reconsidered cannot use it for the younger.
Mishnah case: a man tells the scribe to write a divorce for whichever wife he later chooses; the document is invalid for either wife.
Mishnah case: a husband writes a divorce for his wife, then changes his mind, and the mishnah elaborates on the resulting document.
The Gemara asks what case the first clause of the mishnah then addresses, since it also seems to involve a document written for someone else.
Rav Pappa answers that the first clause concerns scribes writing practice documents, not documents written at someone's request.
Rav Ashi supports this from the mishnah's wording about scribes dictating rather than reading, which points to students practicing.
The Gemara asks what novelty the term moreover introduces in the mishnah's sequence of cases.
A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael: a practice document is invalid, and so is one written for divorce but later abandoned.
The baraita continues: a document written for one wife, or for whichever wife is chosen later, is also invalid against another wife.
The Gemara asks the reason that a divorce document must be written specifically for the woman being divorced.
Without the verse, one might think a document written for divorce but later abandoned could still be valid for another man's use.
The Gemara cites Deuteronomy 24:1, reading the verse as requiring that the document be written for the writer's own divorce.
Hypothetically, and he writes alone might require the user to be the writer; the phrase for her adds that the document must be for a specific wife.
The verse wording for her, meaning for her sake, is cited as the source for requiring a document written for a particular wife.
The Gemara asks why the final clause of the mishnah is needed, since the earlier clauses already establish the requirement.
The final clause teaches that there is no retroactive clarification; the document must be written for the intended wife from the outset.
Mishnah: one who wrote a divorce for the older of two same-named wives and then reconsidered cannot use it to divorce the younger.
The Gemara infers that the younger wife cannot be divorced with it while the older can, since it was written for her.
Rava teaches that one of two same-named men in a city may present a promissory note against outsiders, since the debtor cannot claim it was meant for the other.
Abaye objects that this inference would wrongly let the first same-named man use a divorce, contradicting a mishnah in Bava Batra on identical names.
Abaye asks what Rava can say to explain how the first man may use the divorce document as valid proof of divorce.
The mishnah applies where witnesses see the delivery and confirm the recipient, following Rabbi Elazar, so no concern arises for the other wife.
Rav holds that every invalid divorce document in the mishnah still disqualifies the recipient from marrying a priest, except the first, a practice document.
Shmuel disagrees: even the first practice document disqualifies the woman from marrying a priest.
Shmuel's consistent principle: wherever the mishnah calls a divorce invalid it also disqualifies, and likewise an invalid halitza disqualifies the yevama from the other brothers.
An Eretz Yisrael teaching in the name of Rabbi Elazar: halitza performed on the left foot or at night is invalid yet still disqualifies the yevama.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah ruling: a halitza done by a minor or in an unsuitable shoe is invalid but does not disqualify the yevama from levirate marriage.
Ze'eiri holds that no bill of divorce in the mishnah disqualifies a woman from marrying a priest except the final conditional case.
Rav Asi gives the same ruling as Ze'eiri: only the final conditional bill of divorce disqualifies a woman from marrying a priest.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: even the final bill does not disqualify, since it is not a bill of divorce at all.
Rabbi Yochanan's consistent reasoning, cited from Rabbi Asi: brothers who divided inherited land are treated as buyers who must return portions at the Jubilee.
The Gemara explains the principle must be stated for both inheritance and divorce, since each case has a different reason it might be exempt.
Further explanation: a ruling about inherited fields might be only a stringency, so the divorce case needs its own statement of no retroactive clarification.
Rav Hoshaya asks Rav Yehuda the halakha when a husband tells a scribe to write a divorce for whichever wife exits the gate first.
Rav Yehuda replies that the mishna already teaches this: a document written for whichever wife the husband chooses is unfit, showing no retroactive clarification.
Rav Hoshaya objects with a Pesachim mishna where a father's offering for whichever child goes up first appears to create retroactive clarification.
Rav Yehuda responds that Paschal offerings are irrelevant: Rabbi Yochanan explains the father included all children from the outset, only to motivate them.
Rabbi Yochanan's reading fits the mishna's precise wording, which works only if the children were registered from the outset.
If the children were registered only after slaughter, that would contradict a mishna forbidding registration after slaughter, so that reading must be rejected.
A baraita with a similar incident, where daughters preceded sons, shows the father slaughtered for the sons too, supporting the motivational reading.
Abaye critiques Rav Yehuda's answer: Rav Hoshaya's question concerned others' decisions, while the resolution relied on the husband's own decision, so the cases differ.
Rava resolves that retroactive clarification is accepted or rejected uniformly, regardless of whether the condition depends on oneself or on others.
Rav Mesharshiyya objects that Rabbi Yehuda accepts retroactive clarification when the condition depends on others, contradicting Rava's uniform resolution.
A Tosefta on wine bought from Samaritans shows Rabbi Yehuda rejects retroactive clarification when the condition depends on oneself, supporting the distinction.

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir permits drinking the wine immediately, relying on the tithe separation that will be made later.
Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon prohibit this practice, holding that no retroactive clarification applies here.
Where the outcome depends on others' decisions, retroactive clarification applies, according to the inference drawn from the preceding opinions.
A mishna asks the wife's status in the days between a sick husband's conditional bill of divorce and his death.
Rabbi Yehuda rules she remains a married woman and the bill takes effect at death, implying retroactive clarification for outside decisions.
Rav Mesharshiyya objects to Rava that Rabbi Shimon rejects retroactive clarification for self-dependent conditions but accepts it for others' decisions.
The Gemara answers that the Samaritan wine case shows Rabbi Shimon's view on self-dependent conditions, while the other case accepts others' decisions.
A Tosefta on conditional betrothal, where the father's desire is at issue, is cited as Rabbi Shimon's view that retroactive clarification applies to others' decisions.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara's conclusion: Rabbi Shimon accepts retroactive clarification when the outcome depends on others, since the betrothal hinges on the father's desire.
Rava holds that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon both accept retroactive clarification, whether the condition depends on oneself or on others.
Rava explains the Samaritan wine case with a Tosefta where the Sages questioned Rabbi Meir, implying they would accept retroactive clarification there.
Mishna: a scribe may pre-write the standard formula of divorce documents, leaving blanks for the man's name, the woman's name and the date.
The same pre-writing permission applies to loan documents, leaving blanks for lender, borrower, the sum and the date.
For land-sale documents too, blanks are left for buyer, seller, price, field description and date, due to a rabbinic ordinance.
Rabbi Yehuda invalidates pre-written documents in all cases, while Rabbi Elazar validates them all except divorce documents.
Rabbi Elazar's exception for divorce rests on the verse he writes for her, requiring that the divorce be written for her sake.
Shmuel rules that the blank space must also be left for the essential phrase permitting her to marry any man, following Rabbi Elazar's view.
Rabbi Elazar holds that witnesses at delivery effect divorce and that writing must be for her sake, which grounds Shmuel's ruling.
Shmuel needed to state this explicitly, since the earlier mishna on writing on attached surfaces alone might fit Rabbi Elazar only there.
Likewise the later mishna on deaf-mutes and minors might be read as Rabbi Meir's view that signatories alone effect divorce, so Shmuel must clarify.
The third mishna, explicitly attributed to Rabbi Elazar, would otherwise suggest the first clause is not his view, so each mishna is clarified.
The ordinance is for the benefit of scribes, so documents may be prepared in advance and not rushed, consistent with Rabbi Elazar's view.
Rabbi Yehuda invalidates all pre-written documents, decreeing against the practice lest scribes come to write essential parts in advance too.
Rabbi Elazar decrees only against pre-writing divorce documents, not extending the decree to all other documents that need no specific recipient.
The Gemara objects that the verse he writes for her refers to the essential part of the document, not the standard part, so the derivation fails.
The Gemara answers: the verse on the essential part teaches writing for her sake, and Rabbi Elazar extends that requirement to the standard part too.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks how the mishna can follow Rabbi Elazar when his last clause seems to contradict his first-clause ruling on pre-written standard parts.
The Gemara answers that two tanna'im hold opposing views on Rabbi Elazar's position, so there is no contradiction.
Rabbi Shabbetai reports Hizkiyya: the ordinance prevents quarrels and follows Rabbi Meir, since divorce need not be written for her sake.
Illustration: a scribe may copy a divorce by chance, and the wife may think her husband ordered it, causing a quarrel.
Rav Hisda reports Avimi: the ordinance remedies deserted wives, and it is variously attributed to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar.
Explanation per Rabbi Meir: a husband in anger might hand over a pre-prepared bill and desert her, so a full bill cannot be pre-written.
Explanation per Rabbi Elazar: a husband traveling overseas may find no scribe, so scribes pre-write the standard part to finish quickly.
Mishna: a scribe leaves room for the date; the tanna teaches categorically that this applies equally to marriage and betrothal.
Dating from marriage is understood under either rationale, since it guards against adultery claims or secures the wife's produce.
For betrothal the adultery rationale still applies, but the produce rationale fails, since a betrothed woman has no produce rights.
Rav Amram heard from Ulla that the date serves the child's benefit, though he did not know at first what that benefit was.
A baraita invalidates a bill written for a betrothed woman to be given after marriage; Ulla explains this by a decree against pregnancy confusion.
Rav ruled that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar on pre-written standard parts, and extends the ruling to other documents as well.
Objection: Rav Pappi, citing Rava, invalidates a pre-signed promissory note ratified before testimony, since pre-writing appears falsified.
Reply: Rav Pappi's premise is rejected because of a statement by Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman cites Rabbi Meir validating a found, later-signed divorce; the Rabbis disagree only for divorce, where writing must be for her sake.
Rabbi Asi cites Rabbi Yochanan: a repaid loan note cannot be reused since its lien was forgiven, and appearance of falsehood is not a concern.

27a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a lost bill of divorce brought by an agent is valid only if found immediately, since otherwise it may belong to a same-named person.
Mishna exception: a bill found in a pouch or box the agent recognizes as his, or identified by its contents, remains valid.
The Gemara cites a Bava Metzia mishna on found documents that seems to allow returning them after long delays, contradicting the immediacy requirement.
Rabba resolves the conflict by location: caravan towns raise the namesake concern, and it matters only if two same-named men are known there.
The Gemara notes a contradiction with Rabba's own case: Rav Huna worried about two cities named Sheviri without any established namesake.
Rav Hisda sends Rabba to research the halakha before Rav Huna's questioning, and Rabba finds a relevant source.
Rabba's source: a Bava Metzia mishna says court-authenticated promissory notes go back to their owners without concern about same-named towns.
Objection: Rav Huna's court resembles a caravan place, yet Rabba ruled to return the document, apparently contradicting his earlier locale distinction.
Resolution: if two same-named men are established in one town there is concern, otherwise there is none, so Rabba's ruling is consistent.
Rabba acted on his ruling in a Pumbedita flax-house bill; two versions describe whether that place was caravan-frequented or not.
Rabbi Zeira sets the mishna against a baraita; the mishna says a lost agent's bill is valid only if found immediately.
Baraita contradiction: a woman's bill found in the marketplace is returned to her only if the husband admits writing it, implying other cases are not returned.

27b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita's ruling is restated: if the husband admits writing it, the bill is returned even after a long delay, which Rabbi Zeira reconciles.
Rabbi Zeira's resolution: the mishna refusing return concerns caravan-frequented places, while the baraita permitting it concerns places where caravans are rare.
Two readings of Rabbi Zeira's view: either it matches Rabba only where namesakes are established, or it diverges from Rabba even without them.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Zeira did not argue from the Bava Metzia mishna as Rabba did, given that mishna's more precise language.
Rabbi Zeira could reply that the Bava Metzia mishna supports only an inference; it may instead mean return only if found immediately.
Rabbi Yirmeya's alternative: return is permitted only when the signing witnesses attest they signed no other bill of Yosef ben Shimon.
The Gemara asks what the mishna's point is, since a bill that clearly belongs to the woman obviously must be returned to her.
The teaching is needed to rule out a worry that another bill with identical husband, wife and witness names might exist.
Rav Ashi's alternative: return applies only when the owner describes a clear-cut distinguishing mark, such as a hole next to a specific letter.
Rav Ashi's rationale: returning lost items by marks may be Torah or rabbinic law, so for a bill of divorce only a clear-cut mark suffices.
Rabba bar bar Hana lost a bill in the study hall, offered a mark and his own recognition, and afterward was unsure which one led to its return.

Relatives reply that he is damaging the orphans' property and causing them financial loss.
Rav Naḥman rules: bring witnesses to his damage and I will remove him from the stewardship.
Rav Huna cites Rav: a steward who causes loss is removed, a rule cited from the school of Rabbi Sheila.
Dispute on removing a damaging steward; the halakha is that the court removes him.
Mishna: a steward appointed by the orphans' father takes an oath when he returns the property.
Asks the reason a steward appointed by the father must swear.
He would not have accepted the role unless he benefited from the father, and the oath will not deter him.
Mishna: a steward appointed by the court does not take an oath.
Serving the court is a favor, so imposing an oath would deter people from accepting stewardship.
Abba Shaul reverses the mishna's ruling: the court-appointed steward is the one who swears.
Asks why a court-appointed steward swears.
Court appointment brings public trust in him, so an oath will not deter him from accepting.
A steward appointed by the father does not swear, by Abba Shaul's reasoning.
Serving a father's family is a favor between people, and an oath would deter them from taking it.
Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Abba Shaul, as relayed by Rav Ḥanan bar Ami.
A baraita of R. Eliezer ben Ya'akov: both kinds of steward swear, and the halakha follows him.
Rav Taḥalifa's baraita before R. Abbahu: the father-appointed steward swears because he is paid.
R. Abbahu objects: did you measure how much the steward earns from his efforts?
Reply: say instead that he swears because it is as if he received payment.
Mishna: one who unintentionally causes another's monetary loss through impurity, teruma or libation is exempt, but liable if intentional.
Amoraim dispute the meaning of pouring: Rav says he pours the wine, Shmuel says he mixes it.
Asks why Shmuel does not read the mishna as literal pouring.
One who commits two transgressions with one act is exempt from the lesser penalty, so pouring is not literal.
Rav follows R. Yirmeya: the thief is liable once he lifts the wine, while death is incurred only at pouring.
Asks why Rav, holding pouring, does not say it means mixing.
He could have said to you that mixing libation wine with kosher wine is the other reading.

53a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review
