ranges.en: Shmuel's view: mixing teruma is like rendering impure, and a fine is not derived from a fine in another case.
Asks why the mishna lists all three cases if fines can be derived from one another.
Each case is needed: rendering impure teruma ruins it, but mixing teruma is not otherwise penalized.
Mixing is listed because it is common, while rendering impure is rare and might go unpenalized.
Both cases carry only a fine, so the two-transgressions principle does not apply to either.
Pouring is penalized because of the two-transgressions rule, and Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the fine applies first.
Asks why all three cases are needed under the Tosefta's version, where mixing was added later.
Rendering impure is penalized, but pouring would be exempt under the two-transgressions principle.
Pouring ruins the wine entirely, while rendering impure leaves it usable, so each case is needed.
Rendering impure and pouring involve substantial loss, but mixing causes only minor loss and needs its own ruling.
Ḥizkiyya: by Torah law, the unintentional and the intentional offender are both liable for damage.
Asks the reason Ḥizkiyya holds that unintentional damage is liable.
Damage that is not evident is still categorized as damage, such as rendering property impure.
Asks why the Sages exempt the unintentional offender.
The exemption makes the offender inform the owner, and even the intentional offender will inform him.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: by Torah law the unintentional and intentional offenders are both exempt for damage.
Asks the reason Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that unevident damage is not damage.
Damage that is not evident is not categorized as damage.
Asks why the Sages make the intentional offender liable.
So that no one renders another's pure food impure and then claims exemption, as Rabbi Yoḥanan's view would permit.
The mishna on priests who disqualify offerings intentionally is cited against Ḥizkiyya as a difficulty.
If unevident damage counts, the unintentional priests should be exempt by Torah law, not for the world's betterment.
Rabbi Elazar objects from the one who performs labor with the red heifer's water, exempt by human law.
If unevident damage counts, the same person should be liable by human law too, so the objection stands.
Rabbi Elazar resolves his objection: the labor was incidental, and weighing with the water is not a real task.
Asks: but doesn't Rava say the water of purification is different?

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the water is fit for weighing, given Rava's statement on the matter.
Not difficult: the baraita concerns weighing with the water itself, Rava's case weighing against it.
If he weighs with the water he performs a task, so human-law liability would follow for unevident damage.
Both refer to weighing against the water; the baraita's lapse of attention disqualifies it, Rava's does not.
Rav Pappa objects from a baraita on a robber returning stolen items, refuting Ḥizkiyya's view.
Suggestion: the amoraic dispute parallels a tannaitic dispute, cited from a baraita of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
The amoraim disagree on whether unevident damage counts as damage, as the tannaim do.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: all agree unevident damage is not damage; they dispute penalizing unintentional offenders.
A contradiction arises between Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Yehuda's rulings in the baraita on cooking on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yoḥanan HaSandlar: unintentional cooking may be eaten after Shabbat by others, but never by the cook.
Restating the contradiction within the statements of Rabbi Meir and of Rabbi Yehuda.
No contradiction: Rabbi Meir penalizes unintentional offenses only for rabbinic, not Torah, prohibitions.
Asks: pouring for idolatry is a Torah prohibition, yet Rabbi Meir penalizes unintentional offenders there.
Rabbi Yehuda's rulings are likewise reconciled: the penalty for Torah violations depends on severity.
Asks: pouring is a Torah prohibition, yet Rabbi Yehuda does not penalize unintentional offenders there.
The reversed argument: people avoid idolatry on their own, so no fine is needed for unintentional offense.
Contradiction in Rabbi Meir's rulings on Torah prohibitions, from the baraita on planting trees on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on planting in the Sabbatical Year seems to contradict Rabbi Meir's cooking ruling.
Asks why Shabbat and the Sabbatical Year are distinguished when both prohibitions are Torah law.
Rabbi Meir's reason: Jews count the years of a tree from the Sabbatical Year, so people might think planting is allowed.

54a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Alternative reason: people do not count years from Shabbat, and Jews are suspected only of neglecting the Sabbatical Year.
Asks what Rabbi Meir means by introducing a second, alternative reason.
Objection to the first reason: Shabbat can also be counted, so people would remember a Shabbat planting.
Rabbi Meir's alternative stated again: Jews are suspected of Sabbatical Year neglect, not Shabbat neglect.
No contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's rulings: his place treated the Sabbatical Year as especially serious.
Anecdote supporting this: a man insults another and is answered with the Sabbatical Year's seriousness.
A baraita on restitution for impure teruma, cited to examine Sumakhos's report of Rabbi Meir's view.
Asks why Rabbi Meir invalidates intentional restitution with impure produce, since it is a blessing for the priest.
Rava's emendation: the baraita distinguishes impure and pure teruma, and Rabbi Meir's view is restated.
Rav Aḥa bar Rav Ika: the dispute is whether unintentional offenders are penalized for intentional offenders.
Not comparable: the offender intends to pay, so Rabbi Meir does not penalize him for an unintentional error.
Baraita on blood of an offering sprinkled impure: unintentional sprinkling is accepted, cited against Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Meir replies: the sprinkler intends atonement, a laudatory act, so no penalty applies.
Mishna on tithing produce on Shabbat: unintentional tithing is valid, cited as further support.
Not comparable: the tither intends to repair the produce, a worthy deed, so no penalty applies.
Mishna on immersing utensils on Shabbat: unintentional immersion permits use, a further parallel.
Same distinction: the immerser intends a praiseworthy purification, so the unintentional offender is not penalized.
Contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yehuda on matters prohibited only by rabbinic law.

54b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Perekh nuts that fell and broke: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda forbid them; Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon allow unintentional breakage.
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda penalizes an unintentional breaker, since Torah law nullifies a one-in-two mixture.
Rabbi Yehuda's reason: without a penalty, people would break the nuts deliberately to nullify the Perekh nuts.
A contradiction between Rabbi Yosei's ruling in the mishna on grafted saplings and his ruling on nuts.
Rava and Rabbi Yoḥanan: a person does not render his whole vineyard forbidden for one sapling, so the Sages did not penalize.
Mishna: priests who intentionally disqualify an offering by improper intention are liable to pay its value.
Baraita on credibility: a man who claims he disqualified food or offerings is believed only about the present.
Asks what distinguishes the first clause, where he is believed, from the latter, where he is not.
Abaye: one is believed as long as he can still do what he claims; otherwise he is not believed.
Rava: the latter clause concerns a man who stayed silent at first and spoke only later, which suggests a lie.
Rabbi Ami rules that the claimant is not credible about the pure food, which remains pure.
Rabbi Asi objects, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei: the Torah believes him in such cases.
Asks where the Torah deems him credible.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Bisna: the High Priest on Yom Kippur shows he is believed about improper intent.
Asks how the High Priest's improper intent is known, given that no one may enter the Tent at that time.
Gemara: he is believed because he is presumed to speak truthfully about disqualifying the offering.
Objection: perhaps one saw the High Priest through a small door, so the proof is refuted.
Story: a scribe says he wrote God's name without proper intent, so the Torah scroll is invalid.
Rabbi Ami rules the scribe is believed to lose his wage, but not to invalidate the scroll he sold.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects: he lost wages only for the names, not the whole correctly written scroll.
Rabbi Ami replies: any scroll with improperly intended divine names is worth nothing.
Asks why the scribe cannot correct the names with a reed pen, and whether this follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Baraita on a scribe who erred writing a divine name: Rabbi Yehuda allows correction, the Rabbis do not.
Rabbi Yehuda's leniency applies to a single name only, since correcting every name would look speckled.
Story: a scribe says he did not process the parchment properly, and Rabbi Abbahu rules the scroll is invalid.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how this case differs from Rabbi Ami's ruling about the scribe's credibility.
There the scribe may have lied to distress the buyer, whereas here admitting loss makes him credible.
Mishna: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Gudgeda testifies a deaf-mute woman married off as a minor may be divorced.
Mishna: a minor daughter of a non-priest married to a priest may eat teruma, and her husband inherits her.
Mishna: a stolen beam built into a building is repaid only at its value, as an ordinance for penitents.
Mishna: a sin-offering obtained by robbery, not publicly known, atones for the robber on the altar's behalf.
Rava deduces from the mishna that a husband's secret divorce valid without the woman's consent stands.
Asks why the divorce would not be valid, since the point seems obvious.
Lest he meant to cancel the divorce; but he did not tell the witnesses, and shame led him to disguise it.
Restating the mishna clause on the minor daughter of a non-priest eating teruma.
Inference: a deaf-mute woman married to a priest may not eat teruma.
A decree: a deaf-mute priest might feed teruma to his deaf-mute wife.
Asks why not feed her, since she is like a minor eating forbidden carcasses.
Rather, a decree: the deaf-mute husband might feed teruma to a competent wife, by mistaken analogy.
Asks why she may not eat rabbinic teruma, since rabbinic validity should suffice.
Even rabbinic teruma is forbidden, lest he come to feed her Torah-level teruma.
Restating the mishna clause: a robber who built a stolen beam into a building.
Baraita: Beit Shammai requires demolishing the building, while Beit Hillel requires only the beam's value.
Restating the mishna clause on a sin-offering obtained by robbery.
Ulla: by Torah law, a robbed sin-offering never atones, whether or not the robbery was known.
Despair of recovering stolen property does not by itself transfer ownership, so the robber cannot acquire it.
Asks why the Sages said that an unknown robbery sin-offering atones.
So that priests are not distressed at having sacrificed an animal unfit for the altar.
The Rabbis object to Ulla: the mishna says it atones for the altar, so the rule serves the altar.
Ulla replies: if priests are distressed, the altar stands idle, since they will not sacrifice.
Rav Yehuda: by Torah law it atones whether or not known, since despair lets the robber acquire it.
Asks the reason that despair suffices to transfer ownership.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The reason: so that people do not say the altar consumes stolen property.
Under Ulla's reason the mishna's sin-offering example fits; under Rav Yehuda's, why not also mention burnt-offerings?
Burnt-offerings are wholly burned and need no mention; even sin-offerings are decreed to avoid the same misreading.
Restating the mishna: a sin-offering obtained by robbery, not publicly known, atones for the altar's sake.
Asks why the mishna would not state the reverse, as Rav Yehuda's reading would require.
The mishna does say the reverse: a known robbery sin-offering does not atone, for the altar's benefit.
Rava objects from a mishna on a stolen consecrated animal: karet is cited, which seems to contradict the despair rule.
Rav Sheizevi: karet by rabbinic decree, since the Sages placed the animal in the thief's possession.
Rava asks whether the Sages placed the animal in his possession from the theft or from the consecration.
From the consecration, so that the sinner does not profit from a decree meant to increase his liability.
Mishna: the law of Sicarii did not apply in Judea during the war killings, but applied afterward.
Mishna: buying from a Sicarius then from the owner is void, while the reverse order is valid.
Mishna's first version: the same reversal rule applies to a husband and wife holding the field.
Later court: the buyer from a Sicarius must pay the prior owner one-quarter of the value, unless the owner can buy.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's court: after twelve months with the Sicarius, the first buyer acquires it, paying one-quarter.
Challenge: if no Sicarii operated in the war killings, how could they operate afterward?
Rav Yehuda: the mishna means that during the killings, purchases from Sicarii were confirmed, not voided.
Rabbi Asi's three decrees by the gentile authorities explain why owners transferred land during the killings.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: Jerusalem fell over Kamtza and bar Kamtza, the King's Mountain over a rooster, Beitar over a rispak.
Story: a host mistakenly invites bar Kamtza, his enemy, instead of his friend Kamtza to a feast.
The host tells bar Kamtza to leave; bar Kamtza offers to pay for all he eats and drinks if allowed to stay.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Story: the host repeatedly orders bar Kamtza out of the feast, despite his offers to pay for it.
Bar Kamtza, humiliated, informs the emperor that the Jews rebel and proposes testing them with an offering.
Bar Kamtza blemishes the emperor's calf, which the priests cannot sacrifice nor explain to the authorities.
Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas opposes both sacrificing the blemished calf and killing bar Kamtza, so nothing is done.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the excessive humility of Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas destroyed the Temple.
Nero tests his fate by shooting arrows in four directions, and each one falls in Jerusalem.
Nero hears a child's verse about vengeance on Edom, fears he is God's instrument, and converts; Rabbi Meir descends from him.
Vespasian besieges Jerusalem for three years, and three wealthy men live there.
Explains the names: Nakdimon for the sun shining on him, Ben Kalba Savua for feeding the hungry, Ben Tzitzit for his fringes.
The three wealthy men offer the city wheat and barley, wine and oil, and wood respectively.
Rav Ḥisda's example of valuing the wood key, and his estimate that wood is needed to cook grain.
Zealots prevent peace or battle, then burn the stores of grain, causing a famine.
Story: Marta bat Baitos sends servants for flour of each grade, and each time it is sold out.
Marta steps on dung while going out to find food, and dies of disgust.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai reads Deuteronomy 28:56 about the delicate woman as applying to her.
Alternative account: she ate a fig of Rabbi Tzadok, who fasted for forty years, and died of disgust.
Rabbi Tzadok's fasting, and Marta's gold and silver thrown into the marketplace before she dies.
Ezekiel 7:19 cited: they shall cast their silver in the streets, which Marta's act fulfills.
Abba Sikkara, the zealots' leader and nephew of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, is summoned to meet him in secret.
Rabban Yoḥanan asks how long Abba Sikkara will keep killing the people through starvation.
Abba Sikkara replies that speaking out would get him killed by the zealots.
Rabban Yoḥanan asks for a way to leave the city, however small the chance of salvation.
Abba Sikkara's plan: feign illness, stage a death with something putrid, and have students carry him out.
Rabban Yoḥanan's plan is carried out, and the zealot guards let him out after a feigned pierce and push.
Rabban Yoḥanan greets Vespasian as king, twice, on reaching the Roman camp.
Vespasian objects: you are liable for two deaths, since I am not king and you call me one, and why did you not come earlier.
Rabban Yoḥanan replies to Vespasian's claim, the first part concerning the title.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabban Yoḥanan: you are king, since Jerusalem and the Temple fall only to a king, proven by verses.
Vespasian asks again why Rabban Yoḥanan did not come to him until now, if he is king.
Rabban Yoḥanan replies that zealots within did not allow him to come out.
Vespasian's analogy: one would break a honey barrel wrapped by a snake to kill the snake, so Jerusalem must fall.
Rabban Yoḥanan stays silent, and a verse is read about him concerning those who turn wise men backward.
Isaiah 44:25 cited: the Lord turns wise men backward and makes their knowledge foolish.
What Rabban Yoḥanan should have replied: remove the snake with tongs, and leave the barrel intact.
A messenger from Rome reports the emperor's death, and Vespasian's shoe will not go on or come off.
Rabban Yoḥanan: good tidings are coming, and the remedy is to have someone you dislike pass before you.
Vespasian asks: since you are so wise, why did you not come to see me until now?
Rabban Yoḥanan: I already told you; Vespasian replies that he had also said what he needed to.
Vespasian says he will go to Rome, leave a successor, and grant Rabban Yoḥanan a request.
Rabban Yoḥanan asks for Yavne and its sages, Rabban Gamliel's dynasty, and doctors for Rabbi Tzadok.
Rav Yosef, or some say Rabbi Akiva, applies Isaiah 44:25 to Rabban Yoḥanan.
He should have asked Vespasian to leave the Jews alone this time, rather than the modest requests.
Rabban Yoḥanan made modest requests because he doubted Vespasian would grant more, and hoped for some salvation.
Asks what the doctors did to heal Rabbi Tzadok.
They gave him water with bran, then flour and bran, then flour, slowly widening his stomach.
Vespasian returns to Rome and sends Titus in his place.
Deuteronomy 32:37 is read as referring to Titus, who blasphemed God.
Titus enters the Holy of Holies with a prostitute, sins on a Torah scroll, and cuts the curtain, and blood gushes.
Psalms 74:4 cited: enemies roar in the midst of the meeting place and set up their own signs.
Abba Ḥanan and the school of Rabbi Yishmael read Psalms 89:9 and Exodus 15:11 as rebukes of God's silence.
Titus takes the curtain as a basket, loads the sacred vessels on a ship to be praised in his city.
Ecclesiastes 8:10 is read differently: gathered from the holy place and praised, not buried and forgotten.
Alternatively, the verse is read as written: even buried items were revealed to Titus and his soldiers.
Titus at sea, threatened by a wave, boasts that God's power is only in water; a divine voice answers with a gnat.
Asks why the creature is called a lowly creature.
It has an entrance for food but no exit for excretion.
A gnat enters Titus's nostril and gnaws his brain for seven years, quieted only by the sound of hammering.
Baraita of Rabbi Pineḥas ben Arova: the gnat found in Titus's head at his death was the size of a sparrow.
Abaye's tradition: the gnat had copper mouth and iron claws; dying Titus orders his ashes scattered at sea.
Onkelos bar Kalonikos, Titus's nephew, seeks to convert and raises Titus from the grave by necromancy.
Onkelos asks who is most important in the next world, where Titus now is.
Titus answers: the Jewish people.
Onkelos asks whether he should attach himself to the Jews in this world.
Titus: their commandments are too many; instead battle them in the next world to become chief.
Lamentations 1:5 cited: her adversaries have become the chief, read as anyone who distresses Israel becomes chief.
Onkelos asks what the punishment of that man, Titus, will be in the next world.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Titus's punishment: his ashes are gathered daily, judged, burned, and scattered over the seven seas.
Onkelos raises Balaam from the grave and asks who is most important there, and whether to join the Jews.
Balaam replies with Deuteronomy 23:7: you shall not seek their peace or welfare all your days.
Onkelos asks what the punishment of Balaam will be in the next world.
Balaam: he is cooked in boiling semen, for leading Israel into licentiousness with the daughters of Moab.
Onkelos raises Jesus the Nazarene from the grave by necromancy.
Onkelos asks Jesus who is most important in the next world, and whether he should join the Jewish people.
Jesus: seek their welfare, never their harm, since touching them is like touching the apple of one's eye.
Onkelos asks what the punishment of Jesus will be in the next world.
Jesus: boiling excrement, for mocking the words of the Sages; Balaam sought harm to Israel, Jesus their welfare.
Rabbi Elazar's baraita: see how great the power of shame is, since God destroyed His Temple over bar Kamtza's humiliation.
The King's Mountain custom of a rooster and hen before a wedding, a sign of fruitfulness, led to the rooster's seizure.
Roman soldiers seize the rooster; the residents beat them, and the emperor goes to war against them.
Bar Deroma kills many Romans; the emperor asks God not to give the empire into one man's hands.
Bar Deroma's own words cause his downfall, as he speaks a verse of complaint against God.
Psalms 60:12 quoted: have You not rejected us, O God, so that You go not forth with our hosts.
Asks: did David not also say this same verse?
David asked it as a question, wondering whether it was true; bar Deroma asserted it as fact.
Bar Deroma is killed by a snake in an outhouse; the emperor spares the Jews, but they celebrate and he returns to war.
Rav Asi: three hundred thousand swordsmen massacred the King's Mountain for three days, while weddings continued unaware.
Lamentations 2:2 cited: the Lord has swallowed up all the habitations of Jacob without pity.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rav Asi: King Yannai held six hundred thousand cities in the King's Mountain, three of them excepted.
Explains the three exceptional towns: Evil Town for inhospitality, Shiḥalayim for cress, and Town of Males for birth order.
Ulla saw the place and it could not hold even six hundred thousand reeds, far less so many people.
A Sadducee tells Rabbi Ḥanina that his exaggerations are lies.
Jeremiah 3:19 cited: Eretz Yisrael is the land of the deer, which expands when settled.
Rabbi Ḥanina explains that the land's size varies, expanding when inhabited and contracting when not.
Rav Minyumi, Rav Ḥilkiya and Rav Huna ask anyone to tell what they know of Kefar Sekhanya in Egypt.
Story: a betrothed couple taken captive is married off by gentiles; the man never touches her until his death.
The woman praises him for overcoming his passion more than Joseph, who faced Potiphar's wife only briefly.
Forty se'a of grain cost a dinar; after a drop, a father and son who sinned on Yom Kippur are stoned, and prices recover.
Story: a husband, wanting to avoid a large marriage contract, stages a false adultery with egg white on a sheet.
Bava ben Buta, a disciple of Shammai, says egg white contracts when heated while semen absorbs, which exposes the plot.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef why such righteous people were punished and destroyed.
Rav Yosef: because they did not mourn for Jerusalem.
Isaiah 66:10 cited: rejoice with Jerusalem, all who mourned for her, so mourners share in its rebuilding.
Beitar's custom of planting cedars and cypresses for births and weddings leads to a riot and war after a princess's carriage breaks.
Lamentations 2:3 cited: He has cut off in fierce anger all the horn of Israel.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the eighty thousand battle-trumpet officers of Beitar were killed until their blood reached the Great Sea.
Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer the Great: two rivers in the Yadayim Valley ran with two parts water and one part blood.
Baraita: for seven years gentiles harvested vineyards soaked with Israel's blood without any fertilizer.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Account of Nebuzaradan killing 2,110,000 in the valley and 940,000 on one stone in Jerusalem.
Hosea 4:2 cited: blood touches blood, fulfilled when the slaughter reached Zechariah's blood.
Nebuzaradan finds Zechariah's blood bubbling up, unlike animal blood he brings to compare.
Nebuzaradan demands to know whose blood this is, threatening to comb their flesh with iron.
The priests say a prophet who rebuked them was killed, and his blood has not settled for years.
Nebuzaradan kills the Sanhedrin, youths, virgins and schoolchildren on the blood, but it still does not settle.
Zechariah's voice: the best of them were killed, and the blood settles only once Nebuzaradan stops.
Nebuzaradan repents, reasoning that if one soul's death brought such punishment, his killing of all is worse; he converts.
Baraita: Naaman was a ger toshav, not a convert, whereas Nebuzaradan was a true convert.
Descendants of Haman, Sisera and Sennacherib taught Torah; Shemaya and Avtalyon, Hillel's teachers, were among them.
Ezekiel 24:8 cited as alluding to the blood of Zechariah left uncovered on bare rock.
Genesis 27:22 expounded: the voice of Jacob is Hadrian and Vespasian, hands of Esau are Rome destroying the Temple.
Alternative: no prayer avails without some of Jacob's seed, and no war wins without some of Esau's seed.
Job 5:21 cited: you shall be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, interpreted as hiding from tongue quarrels.
Rav's exposition of Psalms 137:1 and 137:7: God showed David the destruction of both Temples.
Four hundred children taken for prostitution decide to drown themselves; the eldest child urges it.
Psalms 68:23 expounded: bringing back from Bashan and from the depths of the sea refers to those who drown for Heaven.
The girls leap into the sea, and the boys reason a fortiori and follow, fulfilling Psalms 44:23.
Rav Yehuda: the woman and her seven sons refuse idolatry; the first son is quoted the first commandment and killed.
The second and third sons refuse, citing Exodus 20:3 and Exodus 22:19, and are killed.
The fourth and fifth sons refuse, citing Exodus 34:14 and the Shema, and are killed.
The sixth and seventh sons refuse, citing Deuteronomy 4:39 and then the next son's refusal, and are killed.
The next son refuses, citing Deuteronomy 26:17-18, the mutual covenant between God and Israel.
The youngest son answers the emperor's seal offer: if one should honor you, all the more should he honor God.
The mother asks to kiss her son, bids him say to Abraham that she bound seven altars, then dies on the roof.
Psalms 113:9 cited: a joyful mother of children, as she raised her children to serve God.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads Psalms 44:23 as circumcision; Shimon ben Lakish as halakhic demonstration of slaughter.
Shimon ben Lakish: Torah endures only for one who kills himself over it, from Numbers 19:14.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, begins a report about forty se'a of grain.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Phylactery boxes were found on the heads of Beitar's dead, in baskets of forty se'a or three se'a according to a baraita.
The Sages do not disagree: one refers to head phylacteries, the other to arm phylacteries, which differ in size.
Rabbi Asi, Ulla, and Rav Kahana give differing measures of children's brains found on one stone.
Asks which verse this measure is derived from.
Psalms 137:8-9 cited: happy is he who dashes your little ones against the rock.
Lamentations 4:2 cited: the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold.
Asks what it means that they were comparable to fine gold.
Objection: covering them in gold is impossible, since the world holds only two istira weights of fine gold.
Rather, they were so beautiful that they shamed fine gold by their attractiveness.
Roman nobles once used a seal image for conceiving beautiful children, and after the Great Revolt bound Jewish children to their beds.
Story: two such children, one of whom tells the other where this affliction is written in the Torah.
Deuteronomy 28:61 cited: every sickness and plague not written in the book of this Torah.
The first child asks how far he is from reaching this verse in his studies.
Had you gone one and a half columns further you would have reached it, and I would not have needed you.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, citing Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, on the daughters of Beitar's population.
Lamentations 3:51 cited: my eye affects my soul because of all the daughters of my city.
Beitar had four hundred synagogues, each with four hundred teachers and four hundred schoolchildren.
When the enemy entered, schoolchildren stabbed them with pens, and when captured they were burned in their scrolls.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya visits Rome and meets a beautiful child imprisoned there.
The child answers Rabbi Yehoshua by completing Isaiah 42:24 about Jacob given for a spoil.
Rabbi Yehoshua ransoms the child, who soon issues halakhic rulings: he is Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav: the son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha are sold to two masters.
The masters mean to marry the two slaves; each refuses, citing priestly descent, and they weep all night.
At dawn they recognize each other as siblings, and they die in their grief.
Lamentations 1:16 cited: for these things I weep, my eye runs down with water.
Reish Lakish: Tzafenat bat Peniel, named for the gazing at her beauty and her father's service in the innermost sanctum.
Captured, she is raped all night and sold in seven garments; an ugly buyer asks to see her beauty.
The buyer removes the garments; she tears the seventh, rolls in ashes, and appeals to God for the sanctity of His name.
Jeremiah 6:26 cited: O daughter of My people, gird yourself with sackcloth, for the spoiler shall suddenly come.
The lament says upon us, not upon you, since God shares the pain and His name is disgraced with them.
Micah 2:2 cited: they covet fields and houses and oppress a man and his house, the apprentice's story illustrates it.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav introduces a carpenter's apprentice who covets his master's wife.
The master borrows money; the apprentice asks for his wife on loan, keeps her three days, and then claims she was abused.
On the apprentice's advice, the master divorces his wife to pay her marriage contract, and the apprentice marries her.
When the debt comes due, the master serves the couple, weeping into their cups, which some say sealed Israel's sentence.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether a Sicarius's sale is valid when made by bill of sale, and when it passes ownership.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita in accordance with Shmuel: a purchase from the husband then the wife stands only if the wife writes a guarantee.
Objection: let this baraita be a conclusive refutation of Rav, who holds a bill of sale suffices.
Rav could reply that the guarantee also refers to a bill of sale, so no separate guarantee is required.
Baraita: one who buys from a Sicarius and works the land three years before the owner, then resells, cannot be challenged.
Asks what the circumstances of that baraita are.
If the second buyer claims a legal purchase from the owner, the first buyer's possession serves as proof; otherwise neither keeps it.
Rav Sheshet: the second buyer makes no claim, yet courts advance claims for heirs and buyers, but not for the first buyer.
Baraita: land acquired through debt or unjust seizure by a gentile is exempt from the Sicarius laws, but still held twelve months.
Objection: the twelve-month waiting period belongs to the Sicarius laws, which were said not to apply here.
The baraita means property bought from the Sicarius himself must stay with him twelve months.
Rav Yosef holds a tradition that there is no unjust seizure of land in Babylonia.
Objection: unjust seizure of land clearly occurs in Babylonia, so the statement must mean the law is not applied there.
Rather, the owner who never complains to the regional government has waived his claim, so no unjust seizure applies.
Story: Giddel bar Re'ilai pays land tax in advance for three years, and the prior owners then claim the produce.
Rav Pappa considers writing Giddel a document to hold the land for two more years in compensation.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objects that this treats the case like a Sicarius, whose laws do not apply in Babylonia.
Rav Huna instead holds that Giddel placed his money on a deer's horn, so the advance is a gift he cannot reclaim.
Later court's ruling: buyer from a Sicarius pays one-quarter; Rav says one-quarter of the land or money, Shmuel one-quarter of the land.
Asks what the amoraim disagree about in this ruling.
Shmuel holds the Sicarius sold at a quarter below value; Rav holds one-fifth below, explaining the different sums.
Objection from a baraita stating the later court's ruling, with the prior owner choosing land or money.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's court: after twelve months with the Sicarius, the first buyer acquires it, paying one-quarter; this follows Rav.
Rav Ashi: the baraita's one-quarter is of the field's value after the money reaches the owner, not of the sum paid.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The speaker recounts being the youngest court member, yet the court began its vote with his opinion.
Asks why the court began with Rav, not the most learned, when the mishna says to start with the most learned in monetary cases.
Rabba (or Rabbi Hillel) explains that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's court counted from the junior members, since none would contradict him.
No one from Moses to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi combined unparalleled Torah and unparalleled worldly greatness in one person.
Asks: was there not Joshua, unparalleled in both domains?
Joshua's equal in Torah was Elazar, Elazar's was Pinehas, and Pinehas's was the Elders.
Asks: was there not Saul, unparalleled in both domains?
Samuel was Saul's equal in Torah; the claim means no one reigned supreme in both for all his years.
Asks: was there not David, the greatest in Torah and power?
Objection: Ira the Jairite died in David's lifetime, so he was not the leader for all of David's years.
The standard requires being the leading figure in both domains for all the years of leadership.
Asks: was there not Solomon, unparalleled in both domains?
Shimi ben Gera was Solomon's Torah master.
Objection: Solomon killed Shimi at the start of his reign.
The claim is limited to the whole of Solomon's reign, so the objection does not hold.
Shebnah, Hezekiah's equal in Torah, served in his generation.
Objection: Shebnah was killed in the war against Sennacherib.
The claim is that no one matched both domains for all of his years.
Asks: was there not Ezra, the greatest Torah sage and leader?
Nehemiah ben Hacaliah was his equal.
Rav Aḥa bar Rava: from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to Rav Ashi there was no such combined greatness in one person.
Asks: was there not Huna bar Natan, both learned and wealthy, in Rav Ashi's time?
Huna bar Natan was subordinate to Rav Ashi, who surpassed him in both domains.
Mishna: a deaf-mute may transact by gesture; ben Beteira allows lip movements; young children's purchases and sales are valid.
Rav Naḥman clarifies that the dispute concerns only movable property, not divorce, where gestures alone suffice.
Asks whether this is obvious, since the mishna itself limits the rules to movable property.
Rav Naḥman's clarification is needed lest the mishna's limit be read as extending to divorce.
Alternative version: Rav Naḥman says the dispute over movables applies equally to divorce, so the mishna extends to divorce.
Objection: the mishna says these rules apply to movable property, which contradicts the extension.
The mishna should be read as extending the rules to divorce as well as to movable property.
Mishna: young children's purchases and sales of movable property are valid.
Asks up to what age children are included in this enactment.
Rav Yehuda, Rav Kahana, and a baraita give six to seven, seven to eight, and nine to ten, depending on the child's sharpness.
The Sages do not really disagree; each child is judged according to his own understanding.
Asks what the reason is for enacting validity for young children.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: to provide for the child's livelihood, so that a child who must trade does not go hungry.
II Kings 10:22 cited: he who was over the wardrobe brought out garments for the Ba'al worshippers.
Asks what the word meltaḥa means.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: meltaḥa is a garment that can be compressed and then stretched back to full size.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yoḥanan: Bonyam ben Nunyam sent Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi thin linens that fold very small.
Explains that malmala is a fabric that can be compressed and stretched.
Asks up to what amount a young child's mistake in price is cancelled.
Rabbi Yona says Rabbi Zeira: up to one-sixth of the value, like an adult's mistake.
Abaye asks the halakha on a young child's gift.
Rav Yeimar holds that a child's gift is not a valid gift.
Mar bar Rav Ashi holds that a child's gift is a valid gift.
Rav Mordekhai corrects the attribution: Rav Ashi said a child's gift is valid, whether to a dying or a healthy person.
Mishna: for the ways of peace, a priest reads first at Torah readings, then a Levite, then an Israelite, and courtyard joining is placed in an old house.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: for the ways of peace, the nearest pit fills first and trapped game is treated as robbery, which Rabbi Yosei calls full robbery.
Mishna: for the ways of peace, olives beneath a gleaner's tree and a lost item from a minor count as robbery; gentile poor may glean.
Asks from where in the Torah the priest-first rule derives.
Rav Mattana: Deuteronomy 31:9, Moses delivered the Torah to the priests, the sons of Levi.
The Gemara notes this would be needless if the priests were not Levites; so the priests received the Torah first.
Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa: Deuteronomy 21:5, the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come near.
Rav Ashi: I Chronicles 23:13, Aaron was separated to be sanctified as most holy.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba: Leviticus 21:8, sanctify him, giving the priest precedence in study, blessing and portions.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the priest's precedence is a rabbinic enactment, if the Torah itself requires it.
Rav Yosef: it is Torah law, but the reason for precedence is the ways of peace.
Abaye objects: all of the Torah is given for peace, citing Proverbs 3:17, so this is no different.
Abaye explains: the priest's precedence follows Rabba's teaching on yielding precedence to a greater person at a meal.
Rabba: the baraita concerns meals only; in the synagogue, precedence risks quarrels over who is most distinguished.
Rav Mattana: the prohibition on priests yielding precedence applies only to Shabbat and Festivals, not weekdays.
Asks: is it really forbidden, since Rav Huna, not a priest, read the priestly portion on Shabbat and Festivals?
Rav Huna was exempt from concern, since the leading priests of Eretz Yisrael accepted his authority.
Abaye: if no priest is present, the Levite is not given precedence, and if no Levite is present, a priest reads.
Asks: Rabbi Yoḥanan forbids a second priest or Levite from reading after another, so how can Abaye's rule stand?
Abaye's rule refers to the same priest who already read, where no flaw can be suspected.
Asks why Rabbi Yoḥanan worries only about the first priest's status, given equal doubts about both readers.
He speaks where the second reader's father is known to be a priest, so only the first is in doubt.
Asks: then for Levites too, why not assume the second reader's father is a Levite?
The worry is that a father may have married a mamzeret, Gibeonite, divorcee, or ḥalutza, disqualifying his children.
Asks who would be mistaken about the first priest's status.
The concern is for those who leave before the reading ends, not those who stay and see him counted among the seven.
People of the Galilee send a question to Rabbi Ḥelbo, concerning the order of those who follow.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks who may read first from the Torah and reports that Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha was consulted
Order of Torah readers: appointed leaders, qualified scholars, scholars' sons, synagogue heads, then anyone
Galilean question on reading from single-book scrolls in public, escalated to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha
No ready answer; the question was settled in the study hall
Rabbi Yochanan: a Torah scroll missing even one sheet may not be read in public
The proof fails: the defective scroll lacks part of its text, whereas a complete book does not
Rabba and Rav Yosef: no public reading from single-book scrolls, nor haftara scrolls on Shabbat, since such scrolls may not be written
Mar bar Rav Ashi: handling such a scroll on Shabbat is also forbidden, since it is unfit for reading
Rejects that view: handling and reading such a scroll are both permitted
Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish read from an aggada scroll on Shabbat
Objects that aggada, like the Oral Law, may not be written at all
Writing is allowed only because it is impossible to preserve the material otherwise
Psalms verse: it is time to act for the Lord, they have nullified Your Torah
Same reasoning applies to haftara scrolls, since full books cannot always be written
Abaye asks Rabba whether a child may be given a scroll of one portion to study, under each view of Torah composition
Works through the dilemma for each view on whether separate scrolls may be written today
Rabba answers that separate scrolls may not be written, because a partial scroll may not be written
Abaye objects with the Mishna about Queen Helene's gold tablet containing the sota passage
Resh Lakish: the tablet held only the initial letters, so it proves nothing about writing portions
Objects with a baraita saying the priest copies from the tablet, implying the full text was written there
Objects with a second baraita on the same tablet and the same full-text inference
Quotes the Numbers verse on the sota ritual as the text the baraita concerns
Asks how the two baraitot can be reconciled
Resolves it: the tablet alternated full words with initials, so the baraita is not a proof
Baraita: a child may not be given a scroll of one portion, but may if the writer intends to complete it
Rabbi Yehuda's baraita: one may write Genesis up to the flood, and Leviticus up to a point in the book
Rabbi Yochanan: the Torah was given scroll by scroll
Psalms verse: I come with the scroll of the book written for me
Resh Lakish: the Torah was given as one complete book
Deuteronomy verse: take this scroll of the Torah, supporting a complete-book view
Objects that the same verse can be read as supporting the scroll-by-scroll view
That verse refers to the Torah after it had been joined into one unit
Objects that Resh Lakish's view also faces the verse about the scroll written for me
Quotes that verse, in which the book is called a scroll
The verse refers to the whole Torah being called a scroll
Zechariah verse: a flying scroll, showing the Torah is called a scroll
Offers an alternative reading of the flying-scroll image
Rabbi Levi: eight sections were said on the day the Tabernacle was erected, listed in order

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the list of Tabernacle-related sections that must be read in order
Rabbi Elazar: most of the Torah was transmitted in writing, a minority orally
Hosea verse, written for him the greater part of My Torah, cited for Rabbi Elazar
Rabbi Yochanan: most of the Torah was transmitted orally, a minority in writing
Exodus verse, on the basis of these matters I made a covenant, cited for Rabbi Yochanan
Asks why Rabbi Yochanan does not also face the Hosea verse
The Hosea verse is a rhetorical question of bewilderment, not a statement
Asks how Rabbi Elazar handles the covenant verse about oral matters
That verse is stated because oral matters are harder to learn, not because they are more numerous
Rabbi Yehuda bar Nachmani expounds two apparently conflicting Exodus verses about written and oral matters
Reconciles the verses: written matters may not be said orally and oral matters not written; Rabbi Yishmael's school adds a rule
Rabbi Yochanan: God made the covenant with Israel only for the sake of oral teachings
Exodus verse, on the basis of these matters I made a covenant, supports that claim
Mishna: a joint courtyard eruv is placed in the old house where it was placed before, for peace
Asks the reason for keeping the eruv in the old house
Rejects the honor rationale, citing a charity box that was moved between several scholars' houses
The real reason is to avoid suspicion that the owner was stealing
Next mishna: a pit nearest the irrigation channel is filled first, for peace
Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on who drinks first from a river that is dammed
Clarifies the dispute: it concerns dammed water, with each giving a different reason
Shmuel reads the mishna as supporting his view that the nearer party gets first rights
Asks what the mishna teaches, since the point seems obvious
It forestalls the claim that other owners could require the pit owner to dam his pit too
Rav Huna bar Tachalifa: with no halakha settled, the stronger party prevails in practice
Rav Shimi bar Ashi asks Abaye to set a study time
Abaye replies that his time is already fully committed
Shimi proposes studying at night instead
Abaye needs night water for his fields; Shimi offers to irrigate for him by day, and Abaye agrees
Shimi tells each group the opposite view and then dams the river to irrigate Abaye's fields
Abaye rebukes Shimi for acting on two opposing views and refuses to eat that year's produce
Residents of Bei Harmakh dug a channel to divert the river, then returned the water downstream
Upstream owners complain that the diversion harms the river's flow
Abaye suggests digging a little deeper with them to fix the problem
The residents object that deeper digging would dry up their pits
Abaye orders them to remove the diversion and dam it up
Mishna on animals, birds and fish caught in another person's traps, with its nets and snares

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the dispute: for hooks and nets that do not hold the catch, the owner's claim is weaker
Mishna: taking a find from a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor is robbery for peace; Rabbi Yosei calls it full robbery
Rav Chisda: Rabbi Yosei means full robbery under rabbinic law only
Asks what practical difference lies between rabbinic full robbery and robbery for peace
The difference is that a court can compel the robber to return the property
Mishna: olives fallen under a gleaner's tree are robbery for peace; Rabbi Yosei disagrees
A teaching: olives taken from the gleaner's hand are full robbery, since he already acquired them
Rav Kahana sees a man knocking down dates, and he takes and eats some of them
The man objects that the dates were already in his hand, so they were his
Rav Kahana praises the man as from Rabbi Yoshiya's city, citing Proverbs on the righteous as foundation
Mishna: poor gentiles may take gleanings, forgotten sheaves and corner produce, for peace
Baraita: one supports, visits and buries gentiles alongside Jews, for the sake of peace
Mishna: a woman may lend a winnowing basket, sieve, mill and oven to a suspect woman but not help her sift or grind
A ḥaver's wife may help an am ha'aretz's wife sift and grind, but not once water is added
Gentile farm workers may be assisted in the Sabbatical Year, Jews not, and greetings are allowed for peace
Asks why the first clause forbids the help while the latter clause permits it
Abaye: most amei ha'aretz tithe, so the produce is presumed permitted
Rava: the mishna concerns ritual purity under Rabbi Meir's definition of am ha'aretz, not tithes
Objects that the latter clause shows the first clause concerns tithes, not purity
Both clauses concern purity: the first is about ordinary produce, the latter about the priestly dough portion
Introduces a contradiction from another baraita

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: tithed produce may be deposited with those who eat Sabbatical produce or impure food, but not ground for them
Abaye: the baraita concerns a suspect priest who eats teruma impure, a Torah-level prohibition
Asks how then one may deposit tithed produce with such a priest
Raises a contradiction from a baraita permitting teruma deposits with an am ha'aretz Israelite but not with a priest
Rabbi Ile'a: the case is a sealed earthenware vessel, which the suspect priest cannot touch
Asks whether a menstruating wife could still impart impurity by moving the sealed vessel
Rabbi Yirmeya: one case involves produce already susceptible to impurity, the other does not
Raises a contradiction from a mishna: wheat sent to a suspect grinder keeps its tithe status but not its purity status
Asks what the contradiction is, and why the questioner raised it if the answer was already given
The questioner cited the mishna only to set up a contradiction; tithe status is presumed to hold
Raises a contradiction from a mishna on giving food to a mother-in-law who is an am ha'aretz
Rabbi Yehuda: the mother-in-law is ashamed to admit spoiled food, so the concern is specific to her case
Objects with a mishna on an innkeeper, suggesting the concern is not limited to a mother-in-law
The innkeeper justifies swapping food to herself, saying the student should not eat hot food while she eats cold
Objects with a baraita: a ḥaver's wife may grind with an am ha'aretz wife only while she is impure

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that exchange concern is not limited to the mother-in-law and innkeeper cases, since the wife cannot be trusted
Rav Yosef: the wife rationalizes her swap as permitted, so it does not show every am ha'aretz swaps food
Baraita: a ḥaver kneader may keep ordinary dough pure, set aside ḥalla in a basket, and let the am ha'aretz take it
Baraita: the same leniency for an olive presser who sets aside teruma oil in pure vessels belonging to the ḥaver
Asks what the reason for this leniency is
Rabbi Yochanan: it is for the sake of the kneader's and the presser's livelihood
Both cases must be stated, since each alone would suggest the leniency applies only to the other trade
The baraita's ruling restated: the am ha'aretz may take both the dough and the ḥalla
Asks whether the am ha'aretz might still touch the ḥalla and impart impurity
He is told not to touch it, since touching would make the dough untithed again
Asks whether he may not care about the dough becoming untithed again
His evident intent to prepare food properly shows he does care about the dough's status
The same baraita on oil: the presser keeps teruma oil separately in pure vessels of the ḥaver
Asks again whether the am ha'aretz might touch the teruma oil
Ḥalla has a visible marker, the oil is placed in dung, stone or clay vessels that cannot become impure
Asks why the baraita mentions specifically the vessels of a ḥaver
The tanna means the am ha'aretz's own vessels, which also cannot contract impurity
Mishna: one may assist gentiles who work the land in the Sabbatical Year
Objects with a teaching from Rav that one may not hoe with a gentile or double the greeting
Only words of encouragement are permitted, such as saying be strong, not actually helping
Restates Rav's rule: one may not double the greeting of shalom to a gentile
Rav Ḥisda greets gentiles first, and Rav Kahana waits, to avoid doubling; the mishna permits greetings
Asks why the mishna needs to permit asking after gentiles if encouragement is already allowed
Rav Yeiva: the greeting is needed only on their holidays
Baraita: one may not enter a gentile's home on his holiday to greet him, and in the market greets softly
Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda sit as the Sage Geneiva passes by
One proposes that they stand up for Geneiva, since he is a son of Torah
The other objects that they should not stand before an argumentative person
Geneiva greets them twice as kings, saying peace be upon you, kings
Asks from where they know that Sages are called kings
Proverbs verse: through me kings rule, showing the Torah scholars are called kings
Asks from where the greeting to kings is doubled
Rav Yehuda's teaching in Rav's name: the greeting to a king is doubled
Chronicles verse: Amasai's words of peace to David, peace, peace, showing a doubled greeting to kings
Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda offer Geneiva something to taste
Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: one may not taste anything before feeding one's animal
Deuteronomy verse: I will give grass for your animals, and then you shall eat and be satisfied
Closing marker that ends the chapter

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a husband may retract a delivery agency until the get reaches the wife, but not a receipt agency she set up
Mishna: if the husband rejects receipt by her agent and says deliver, he may retract until the get reaches her
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: even a wife's instruction to take the get creates an agency that cannot be retracted
Rav Aḥa asks Rav Ashi why the mishna allows retraction
Rav Aḥa infers that a delivery agent counts as a receipt agent, so saying deliver equals saying acquire
Rejects that inference: the mishna does not equate delivery with receipt
The wording about receipt is needed because a husband cannot appoint a receipt agent for his wife
Cites the mishna on a wife's receipt agent, which cannot be retracted
Asks whether the rule differs for receipt versus delivery, or not
Brings a further mishna proof: the husband's retraction after delivery language is allowed
Infers from the mishna that saying deliver is like saying acquire, since the husband only said I do not want
Suggests the mishna may concern an expression of handing over, so the inference fails
It is clear that a man can be a delivery agent and a woman a receipt agent, but the reverse is unsettled
Asks what the halakha is when a man is a receipt agent and a woman a delivery agent
Offers another mishna proof that a single agent valid for receipt is valid for delivery
Asks whether the mishna may refer to one agent after all
No: it refers to two agents, a male delivery agent and a female receipt agent
Raises a further proof from the same mishna, with one agent valid for both roles
A man may be a receipt agent, as a father receives a get for his minor daughter
Raises the dilemma of whether a woman may be a delivery agent
Rav Mari resolves it from a mishna: women may bring a get to the wife even when they cannot testify to death
Rav Ashi resolves it from the latter clause: the woman herself may bring her get if she declares it in court
Case: a husband says he will hand the get to the agent as the wife said, and the dispute on who controls it
Rav Naḥman, citing Rav: even if the get reached her, she is not divorced, because it rests on the agent's word
Reasons that if the wife's word governed the agent's status, she should be divorced once the get reaches her
Rav Ashi says the two cases cannot be compared

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Naḥman, citing Rav: once the get reaches her hand she is divorced; the husband relies on her designation
Explains Rav Naḥman's ruling: the agent negates his own agency by declaring himself a receipt agent only
Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya objects from the mishna that the divorce fails only where the husband retracts
Asks why she is divorced when the husband cannot appoint a receipt agent
Once he decides to divorce, his intent is that the divorce take effect however it happens
Rejects the comparison: there the husband knows he cannot appoint a receipt agent, so the cases differ
Rava objects from a mishna on a minor girl's agent, extending the same reasoning
Rejects that comparison too: a minor cannot appoint an agent, so the husband knows no agency exists
Objects from a baraita where the husband's responses decide whether the divorce takes effect on receipt
Asks what the baraita implies, and infers from it that the husband relies on the agent's statement
Rejects the comparison: in Rav Naḥman's case the husband explicitly ties the agent to her words
Baraita: if the husband says acquire or receive, he cannot retract once the get is handed over
Rabbi Natan: if the husband says deliver, he may retract until the get reaches her; receipt terms bar retraction
Rabbi Meir: in all cases the husband cannot retract once the get is handed over
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: only an explicit I do not want with deliver lets him retract
Asks why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view is the same as the first tanna's
Either Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi adds the explicit words, or he identifies the first tanna as himself
Raises a dilemma: is Rabbi Natan's case comparable to a case of the husband saying acquire
Resolves the dilemma from the mishna on the receipt agent and delivery agent

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the mishna's case is Rabbi Natan's view on here you are, versus Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
Brings another mishna proof: deliver with I do not want allows retraction, but deliver alone does not
Repeats the question of whether the mishna concerns Rabbi Natan's view or Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's
Cites a baraita where Rabbi Natan treats here you are as comparable to acquire, inferring the same
Rav's ruling: the agent is both the husband's delivery agent and the wife's receipt agent, affecting ḥalitza and levirate
Asks whether Rav was uncertain about deliver versus acquire, given his ruling on a loan
Rav's ruling on a loan is cited as showing that deliver counts as acquire
Distinguishes: a loan involves monetary uncertainty and is lenient, a divorce involves ritual uncertainty and is strict
Rav holds a woman cannot appoint a receipt agent for the husband's agent; Rabbi Ḥanina allows it
Asks what Rav's reason is
Either it would look like contempt for the husband, or it is a decree like the courtyard case
Asks what difference lies between the two reasons
The difference is whether she appointed the agent before the husband's agent acted, and contempt remains a concern
A woman holds a divorce from an agent while kneading; Rav Naḥman would rule the divorce takes effect
Rava objects: the agency never returned to the husband, so the agency was not completed
Rabbi Ami rules that the agency did not return to the husband, so no divorce takes effect
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba says the matter will be considered before a response
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba: the question remains uncertain for us as it was for them
Concludes the uncertainty concerns forbidden relations, so the stringent ruling applies: ḥalitza, no remarriage
Incident: Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta required a second get and ḥalitza in one case
Asks how a second get and ḥalitza can both be required, since they are mutually exclusive
A get while the husband lives, and ḥalitza if he dies without giving one
A misnamed get written by witnesses is invalid, and the witnesses cannot rewrite it since their agency is done
Rabba objects: the husband told them to write a valid get, so their agency was not performed
Rabba's ruling: a proper get that was lost discharges the witnesses, but an invalid one does not
Rav Naḥman objects: the husband did not tell them to keep the get in their pockets
Rav Naḥman's ruling: in such cases witnesses may write and hand over a get even a hundred times
Rava asks whether witnesses told to hand a get to an agent keep their agency for rewriting
Ravina asks whether the added phrase that he deliver it extends their agency; left unresolved
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: even take my get for me creates receipt agency, so retraction is not allowed
Baraita: all expressions such as take, lift, or hold for me count as receipt
Mishna: a woman who appoints a receipt agent needs two pairs of witnesses for the get's receipt and tearing

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna remnant: one witness from each pair and one more joins them to form the second testimony
Asks who is credible when a husband says deposit and the third party says divorce
Rav Huna: the husband is credible; Rav Ḥisda: the third party is credible
Each side's reasons: a husband who meant divorce would hand the get directly; the husband trusted the third party
Rabbi Abba objects from a baraita where a third party is more credible than both litigants
Money can be forgiven, so the rule does not extend to divorce, where forgiveness is impossible
Asks why a baraita says the same halakha applies to gittin, and whether gittin means divorces or monetary documents
The two baraitot are separate, so gittin may refer to monetary documents in one and not the other
Mishna on witnesses who testify to a woman's receipt agent and the tearing of the get
Asks why witnesses are needed if the third party can be trusted to show the get was torn
The third party is trusted only while he holds the get, which is no longer the case once it is torn
Asks why witnesses are needed for the tearing, since the get was already in the third party's hand
Rabba: the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar, for whom witnesses of delivery effect the divorce
Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: the tearing was required during the period of persecution, to hide the evidence
Rabba: Rav Huna concedes that if the wife reports the third party's account, she is credible
Asks whether there is any case where the third party is not credible but the wife is
Rabba: she is credible when she says her husband gave the get to the agent, by the principle of miggo
Rabbi Yochanan: where husband and third party both say divorce but she says it was lost, two witnesses are needed
Asks why the third party should not be trusted, since he holds the get for divorce
The get is no longer in his hand, so trusting him does not follow
Asks whether the husband should be trusted, since Rabbi Yochanan trusts one who says I divorced
In this case the husband never says I divorced her; he only handed over the get
Asks whether an agent is presumed to carry out his task, as in Rabbi Yitzchak's betrothal example

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The agent presumption applies only where it leads to stringency, not to leniency
Asks whether the wife herself should be believed when she says her husband divorced her, per Rav Hamnuna
Her word is accepted only without supporting evidence; where the husband and third party back her, she needs the get
Mishna: a betrothed girl or her father may receive her get; Rabbi Yehuda says only the father, and a girl who cannot safeguard it cannot be divorced
Asks what the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda disagree about
The Rabbis: the Merciful One gives the girl an extra hand; Rabbi Yehuda: with her father alive her hand counts for nothing
Mishna continuation: a woman who cannot safeguard her get cannot be divorced
Baraita: a minor who knows how to safeguard her get may be divorced, and one who keeps other items with it qualifies
Asks what the tanna means by safeguarding her get and something else
Rabbi Yochanan: she safeguards something else mistaken for the get, after losing the get itself
Rav Huna bar Manoaḥ objects that such a girl is merely an imbecile
Rav Huna bar Manoaḥ, citing Rav Aḥa: she distinguishes her get from other items and keeps only the get
Rabbi Asi: a child who distinguishes value acquires for himself but not for others, until he understands ownership
Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel said this and that are one, so no developmental distinction applies
Rav Ḥisda explains: both children acquire only for themselves, regardless of developmental stage
Rav Ḥinnana of Vardania objects with the mishna on merging alleyways through a barrel and a Hebrew maidservant
Asks what the status of such a maidservant is, if she is not of majority age
Suggests a minor can acquire for others, since the mishna teaches that she acquires for others
Merging alleyways is a rabbinic ordinance, where leniency allowed a minor to acquire for others
Rav Ḥisda: Rav Ḥinnana was silent because the Sages' ordinances can be relied on in this way

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Hinnana was silent because the parallel-to-Torah principle covers only ordinances rooted in Torah law
Rav Avya objects with a Ma'aser Sheni mishna where a father's agent redeems tithes for a child, implying minors acquire for others
Asks what the circumstances of that maidservant are if she has reached majority
The case concerns tithes today, a rabbinic matter where leniency applies
Asks whether a Hebrew maidservant exists at all today
A baraita: Hebrew servitude applies only while the Jubilee applies, so the case must be a rabbinic unperforated pot
Rava: three developmental stages for a minor boy and girl, covering acquisition, marriage, vows, and selling property
Mishna: a minor girl's receipt agent is invalid, so the husband may retract and the agent only delivers
Mishna: if the father appoints a receipt agent for his minor daughter, the husband cannot retract
Mishna: a delivery agent who gives the get in another place invalidates it when told the place; otherwise it is valid
Mishna: a receipt agent who takes the get elsewhere is invalid; Rabbi Elazar validates it
Asks why the first clause agrees with the first tanna while the latter clause disagrees with him
The husband divorces by choice and insists on the place; the wife is divorced against her will and only indicates it
Mishna on a priest's wife: she eats teruma until the get reaches her, unless she appoints a receipt agent
Asks whether a get taken in another place is valid, given the earlier ruling that it is not
The halakha concerns a place where she named a city and the agent finds the husband elsewhere, so any place suffices

65b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The divorce is not valid until the get reaches the named town of Mata Meḥasya
Asks why Rabbi Elazar's immediate prohibition is needed, since naming a place is obviously just indicating it
Rabbi Elazar's ruling covers an agent who went the wrong way and might meet the husband en route
Baraita on an eiruv made with dates versus dried figs: one version says valid, the other says invalid
Rabba reconciles: the Rabbis require exact compliance with instructions, while Rabbi Elazar does not
Rav Yosef: both follow the Rabbis, but the deviation matters only when it concerns the principal's own fruit
Abaye objects with a parallel baraita on a tower versus a dovecote, asking what distinguishes the fruit
The instruction concerned where the fruit lies, and the two baraitot differ on whose fruit it was
Mishna: write a get or a letter and give it to her, but phrases like release or treat her well do not divorce
Baraita: send, separate, or banish signal divorce; Rabbi Natan accepts patruha but not pitruha
Rava: Rabbi Natan is Babylonian and distinguishes pitruha from patruha, while the Eretz Yisrael tanna does not
Raises a dilemma about whether remove, abandon, unbind, let be, or treat as custom suffice for divorce
A baraita settles at least one: treat her according to custom does not effect divorce
Mishna: a man led out to execution or setting sail may order a get to be written, and even a gravely ill man
Narrative: Geneiva, led out to execution, bequeaths four hundred dinars to Rabbi Avina from his wine

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Huna: a get is like a deathbed gift, revocable if the giver recovers
Parallel: as a deathbed get needs no delivery words, so a deathbed gift needs no acquisition, allowing collection
Rabbi Abba objects that a get is pointless after death, unlike a gift, so the parallel fails
Asks how Rabbi Abba's difficulty fits with the rule that a deathbed gift requires acquisition
Here the gift is a mitzva to fulfill the deceased's instruction, so acquisition is not required
Asks what difficulty Rabbi Abba has if a mitzva of imminent death needs no acquisition
Asks what Geneiva meant by four hundred dinars from wine, a phrase that seems ambiguous
Rabbi Zeira: the wine designation secured Rabbi Avina's access to the estate; Eretz Yisrael agreed
Mishna: a man in a pit may have anyone who hears him write and deliver a get, though they cannot see him
Asks whether the voice from the pit could be a demon
Rav Yehuda: if they saw a human-shaped figure, the concern is removed
Objects that demons can take human form and have a shadow, and their shadows could mislead
Rabbi Ḥanina: demons have a shadow but not a shadow of a shadow
Asks whether a rival wife might be the source of the voice to cause a false divorce
A teaching from Rabbi Yishmael's school: in danger, a get may be written and delivered despite unfamiliar parties
Mishna: a healthy man who says write a get but not give it is presumed to mock, so the get is invalid
Mishna: a healthy man falls from a roof after ordering a get; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel validates it only if he fell by his own will
Asks whether the incident contradicts the ruling that a healthy man's get is invalid
The mishna is incomplete: if his later actions show intent to divorce before dying, the get is valid
A man asks two men in a synagogue to write a get; the schoolteacher dies, and his son was among those present
Asks whether people appoint a son as agent in his father's presence
Rav Naḥman says no, Rav Pappi says yes, and Rava rules that people do appoint a son in his father's presence
Mishna: if a man tells two people to give a get to his wife, they may do so

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: when a man tells three people to write and deliver his divorce, they must write it themselves as a court, per Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Ḥanina of Ono's tradition, received in prison: the three designated people may pass the task on, since they form a court.
Rabbi Yosei's counter-tradition: even a directive to the Jerusalem High Court requires the judges to learn and write the get themselves.
Mishnah for ten recipients: one writes and the rest sign; if one of them dies, the divorce is void.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reports a question to Shmuel: if two were told to write, and a scribe wrote and they signed, is it valid?
Shmuel rules that she must leave her second husband, but the matter requires further study.
Asks what exactly the phrase 'the matter requires study' means and which uncertainty is meant.
Proposed explanation: the doubt is whether verbal instructions pass to another agent, so the agents could appoint the scribe.
Objection: Shmuel ruled that verbal directives cannot be delegated, so he had no doubt on that point.
Corrected reading: the real dilemma is whether the husband meant their signatures or the writing of the get itself.
Asks why Shmuel did not resolve the doubt from the mishna about two or three people told to write and deliver.
The mishna settles it: the instruction obviously means writing the bill, as its latter clause teaches.
Support from the mishna's latter clause: Rabbi Yosei's ruling that High Court members must learn to write the get themselves.
Objection: if signatures are meant, it is absurd, since courts already know how to sign their names.
Reply: yes, a new court can exist whose members have not yet set a recognizable signature.
If signatures are meant, a scribe-written get should be valid, yet Shmuel ruled verbal directives cannot be delegated.
Sages' reply: this is like telling others to write, and Rabbi Yosei concedes that case.
Challenges the reply: does Rabbi Yosei really concede the 'tell another to write' case?
Objection from a mishna: a scribe's writing verified by one witness is valid, which seems to support delegation.
Rabbi Yirmeya replies that the mishna concerns the scribe's signature, not his writing, so it is no objection.
Rav Ḥisda explains the mishna follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds verbal directives cannot be delegated, so no unauthorized signing is feared.
Objection: if Rabbi Yosei conceded, a pitfall follows in a case where a man told two people to write.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Agents told to have a scribe write and witnesses sign; an unauthorized witness signing is the feared flaw, making the get invalid.
Reply: since the Master holds such a get valid, the case is rare, so the Sages issue no decree against it.
Objection: the husband might tell two people to sign while the scribe also signs, so the same concern arises.
The Sages reply: this too is valid but should not be done, since such cases are uncommon and need no decree.
Reply: this works if one holds valid but not to be done; for one who permits it ab initio, nothing more needs saying.
Explains the dispute: Rabbi Yosei held two rulings; Shmuel accepts one and rejects the other about delegating agency.
Shmuel cites Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: halakha follows Rabbi Yosei that verbal directives cannot be delegated to an agent.
Rabbi Shimon asks his father why he ruled like Rabbi Yosei when Rabbi Meir and Ḥanina of Ono disagree.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says Rabbi Yosei's reasoning accompanies his statements, so his view is most reliable.
A baraita praising the Sages' distinct qualities, supporting the claim that Rabbi Yosei's reasoning accompanies his rulings.
Explains the baraita: Rabbi Shimon removed only chaff, and his rulings are the finest of Rabbi Akiva's.
Rav Huna cites Rav: the case of two people told to write and sign is valid but must not be done in Israel ab initio.
Ulla asks Rav Naḥman: if it is valid, why must it not be done in Israel?
Rav Naḥman: we fear the woman might hire witnesses, unknown to the husband, to forge the get.
Asks: but are we really concerned about such forgery?
Objection from a baraita: the Sages were not concerned about forgery on a sale deed or a woman's get.
Reply: they would not forge themselves but would tell another to forge, who acts unknowingly.
Introduces another case: a man tells two people to have a scribe write and them sign the get.
Rav Ḥisda: valid, but should not be done ab initio.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana: valid, and it may be done ab initio.
Rav Naḥman: valid, but should not be done ab initio.
Rav Sheshet: valid, and it may be done ab initio.
Rabba: valid, but should not be done.
Rav Yosef: valid, and it may be done.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Notes that some reverse the attributions of Rabba and Rav Yosef's opinions on this matter.
Restates the mishna's case: a man tells ten people to write and give a bill of divorce to his wife.
A baraita on the ten-person case: one writes or delivers on behalf of all, depending on the wording used.
Poses a dilemma: if he enumerates them by name and says write, may one of them write for all?
Rav Huna holds that naming them by name is not comparable to saying 'All of you write'.
Rabbi Yoḥanan, citing Rabbi Elazar of Rome, holds that naming them by name is comparable to 'All of you write'.
Rav Pappa says they do not disagree: each opinion addresses a different case, whether all or only some are named.
Rav Yehuda instituted a formula for a get given before many: say each of you, or all of you, so no invalidity arises.
Rava objects: the long formula may be truncated to 'All of you', which would invalidate the bill if one fails.
Rava's fix: the husband must say each one may write, each pair may sign, each one may deliver; never 'all of you'.
Chapter-closing formula ('Hadran alach') marking the end of this chapter and the start of the next.
Mishna: a man with temporary insanity (kordeyakos) whose instruction is void, and a mute man whose nod is valid after testing.
Asks what kind of temporary insanity the mishna means.
Shmuel: it refers to one afflicted by drinking new wine straight from the winepress.
Asks why the tanna did not state explicitly the case of new wine, if that is what is meant.
The mishna teaches a new fact: the demon causing this insanity is named Kordeyakos.
Asks what practical difference the demon's name makes.
The difference is in writing an amulet, which must include the demon's name to protect the patient.
Asks what the remedy for this illness is.
Remedy: eat red meat roasted over coals and drink wine diluted with a large amount of water.
Abaye's mother's remedies for fevers by age, ending with cold water, bloodletting, and a black hen for old fevers.
Remedy for fever: roasted red meat with diluted wine; for chills, roasted fatty meat with undiluted wine.
Account of the Exilarch's household afflicting Rav Amram with snow, and the remedy that he secretly preferred.
Yalta, Rav Naḥman's wife, treats Rav Amram by immersing him in bathhouse water, causing skin spots.
Rav Yosef warmed himself by grinding at millstones, and Rav Sheshet by lifting beams: labor warms its master.
The Exilarch asks Rav Sheshet why he does not eat with them.
Rav Sheshet: the Exilarch's servants are not careful, as they are suspected of eating a limb cut from a living animal.
The Exilarch asks who says this is so.
Rav Sheshet answers that he will show him the truth now.
Rav Sheshet orders his servant to steal a leg from the Exilarch's servants' slaughtered animal.
The servant brings the leg; the servants set out only three legs, and they replace the missing one from another animal.
Rav Sheshet asks: did this animal have only three legs?
The servants cut a leg from another living animal; Rav Sheshet has his servant produce the stolen leg as well.
Rav Sheshet asks: did this animal have five legs?
The Exilarch proposes that the meat be prepared in his servant's presence, so Rav Sheshet may eat without concern.
Rav Sheshet agrees; a table is set and the meat is brought before him.
The servants hide a small bone in the meat to choke Rav Sheshet, who, blind, feels it and wraps the meat.
After he eats, the servants report to the Exilarch that Rav Sheshet did not eat the meat they gave him.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates that a silver cup was stolen, everyone was searched, and the meat was found wrapped in Rav Sheshet's scarf.
The Exilarch's servants accuse Rav Sheshet of refusing to eat only to afflict them.
Rav Sheshet replies that he ate and tasted the flavor of white spots, which is why he did not eat.
The servants object that they did not prepare any animal with white spots that day.
Rav Sheshet says to check the spot, citing Rav Ḥisda that black spots in white skin are an affliction.
They check and find the animal afflicted; then a pit is dug, and Rav Ḥisda signals Rav Sheshet from behind.
Rav Sheshet asks a child to recite a verse he studied that day.
