The child cites II Samuel 2:21, 'turn to your right or to your left', as a warning about the hidden pit.
Rav Sheshet asks his blind servant what he sees ahead.
The servant replies that he sees a mat that was placed on the ground.
Rav Sheshet instructs him to turn away from the mat and go around it.
Rav Ḥisda asks how Rav Sheshet knew the pit was there.
Rav Sheshet lists his suspicions: Rav Ḥisda's signal, the child's verse, and servants not acting to a high standard.
Ecclesiastes 2:8 is cited, with its words explained as musical instruments, pools, and bathhouses.
Babylonian and Western translations of 'shidda' and 'shiddot': male and female demons, or carriages.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says there were three hundred kinds of demons in Shiḥin, but he does not know what a demon is.
Restates the Babylonian interpretation: 'shidda' and 'shiddot' refer to male and female demons.
Asks why Solomon needed male and female demons to write Ecclesiastes.
I Kings 6:7 is cited: the Temple was built with stone cut without iron tools, supporting the need for demons.
Solomon asks the sages how he should cut the stones without iron.
The sages reply that there is a creature called the shamir, which Moses used to cut the ephod stones.
Solomon asks where the shamir can be found.
Torment a male and female demon together, since they may reveal the location under suffering.
The demons reply that they do not know where the shamir is, and suggest that Ashmedai, king of demons, may know.
The demons' suggestion is spelled out: Ashmedai may know where the shamir is.
Solomon asks where Ashmedai is.
Ashmedai is on a mountain, in a sealed water pit, and studies in heaven and on earth each day.
Solomon sends Benayahu, who arranges a pit of wine that traps Ashmedai when he drinks.
Ashmedai checks his seal, finds the pit filled with wine, and resolves not to drink it.
Proverbs 20:1 is cited: wine is a mocker, and whoever wallows in it is not wise.
Hosea 4:11 is cited: harlotry, wine and new wine take away the heart.
Thirsty, Ashmedai can no longer resist, drinks until intoxicated, and falls asleep.
Benayahu descends from the tree, throws the chain around Ashmedai, and Ashmedai struggles against it.
Benayahu tells him that God's name is upon him, so he must not tear the chain.
Bound, Ashmedai is led to Jerusalem and knocks down a palm tree, a house, and a widow's small shack.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrates that Ashmedai, cornered by the woman's plea, bent away and broke a bone, which he links to a verse.
Proverbs 25:15 is cited: soft speech can break a bone, which Ashmedai applies to his own injury.
Ashmedai's deeds: he guides a blind man and a drunk, cries at a wedding, laughs at a shoemaker's and a sorcerer's remarks.
Ashmedai arrives in Jerusalem but is kept waiting three days before being brought to Solomon.
On the first day, Ashmedai asks why the king does not want to see him.
He is told the king drank too much; Ashmedai's brick gesture is read by Solomon as 'give him more to drink'.
On the second day, Ashmedai again asks why the king does not want to see him.
He is told the king ate too much; Solomon reads the removed brick as 'take his food away from him'.
After three days Ashmedai measures four cubits with a reed and rebukes Solomon that a man gets only his grave.
Solomon says he wants nothing from Ashmedai, only the shamir, which he needs to build the Temple.
Ashmedai says the shamir was given not to him but to the sea's minister, who gives it only to the wild rooster.
The wild rooster carries the shamir to rocks, splits mountains, and plants seeds there; hence the translation 'cutter of mountains'.
They find the rooster's nest covered with glass; a servant's clump of dirt makes the rooster drop the shamir, and it kills itself.
Benayahu asks why Ashmedai guided the blind man onto the correct road.
Ashmedai says a heavenly proclamation calls that man completely righteous, so helping him earns him the World-to-Come.
Benayahu asks why Ashmedai guided the drunk man onto the correct road.
The heavenly proclamation calls that man wicked, so Ashmedai helped him to consume his reward in this world.
Benayahu asks why Ashmedai cried at the wedding.
Ashmedai knew the groom would die within thirty days, leaving his widow to wait for a minor yavam to perform ḥalitza.
Benayahu asks why Ashmedai laughed at the man ordering shoes for seven years.
Ashmedai says that man has only seven days left to live, so he has no need for shoes lasting seven years.
Benayahu asks why Ashmedai laughed at the sorcerer performing magic.
The sorcerer sits on the king's treasury; Ashmedai says he should use magic to learn what lies beneath him until the Temple was built.
One day Solomon stood alone with Ashmedai and spoke to him.
Numbers 24:8 is cited, with the Sages' reading that the lofty horns are angels and the wild ox refers to demons.
Solomon asks in what way Ashmedai is greater than human beings.
Ashmedai asks for Solomon's ring in exchange for showing his strength; he swallows it and throws Solomon four hundred parasangs away.
Solomon quotes Ecclesiastes 1:3 and 2:10 about the profit of toil, which he spoke at that moment.
Asks what the expression 'and this' refers to, if it points to an object in hand.
Rav and Shmuel disagree: one says it is Solomon's staff, the other his cloak, which he showed while collecting charity.
Ecclesiastes 1:12 is cited: 'I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem', which Solomon said as he went about.
When he came to the Sanhedrin, the sages heard him and took note.
The sages ask whether an imbecile fixates on one matter, and so whether this man is Solomon, and ask Benayahu whether the king needs him.
Benayahu replies that the king does not need him.
The sages send to the queens to ask whether the king comes to them.
The queens reply that he does come.
The sages ask the queens to check whether his feet are human.
The queens reply that he always wears socks, so his feet cannot be seen.
The queens report the imposter's demands; the Sanhedrin concludes he is not Solomon and summons the real king, who makes him flee.
Even so, Solomon was afraid of Ashmedai.
Song of Songs 3:7-8 is cited, describing Solomon's bed guarded by sixty warriors with swords from fear in the nights.
Rav and Shmuel disagree about the story: one holds Solomon never regained his kingship, the other that he did.
Headache remedy: boil cypress, willow, myrtle, olive, poplar, sea willow and cynodon, and pour three hundred cups on each side.
Alternative headache remedy: boil a single white rose and pour sixty cups on each side of the head.
Migraine remedy: slaughter a wild rooster with a silver dinar over the painful side, and hang it on the doorpost.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Eye remedy: grind a dried seven-colored scorpion with stibium and apply three eyebrushes to each eye, no more or the eye bursts.
Night blindness: tie a leg to a dog's leg, have children throw shards, eat meat from seven houses, then untie and recite a formula.
Day blindness: roast seven spleens on a bloodletter's shard, with the patient and another exchanging words, then break the shard.
Nosebleed: have a priest named Levi write his name backward, or else an ordinary man writes a formula backward.
Nosebleed alternative: write a sentence about tasting water, burn plants into ash, and place wool strings in the nostrils.
Nosebleed alternative: watch a stream flowing east to west, stand astride it, and place clay-soaked wool strings in the nostrils.
Nosebleed alternative: sit under a gutter, have water poured over him, and recite that the blood should cease like the water.
Blood from the mouth: test with a wheat straw; if blood sticks it comes from the lungs and is treatable, otherwise the liver.
Rav Ami objects from a mishna: a punctured lung makes an animal a tereifa, which seems more serious than a liver defect.
Rav Ashi replies that since the blood comes from the mouth, the liver has dissolved and the patient will not survive.
Asks what the remedy is when the blood comes from the lungs.
Remedy: cook seven fistfuls each of beets and leeks, plus other herbs and firstborn intestines, then drink strong beer.
Rabba bar Rav Huna: for toothache, grind a single-clove garlic with oil and salt, place it on the thumbnail, and seal it with dough.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: for gums, hold chamomile root in the mouth, and boil bran, lentils and fenugreek to draw out the pus.
For blisters: a friend blows white cress through a straw into the mouth, and dirt from a bathroom shade kneaded with honey is eaten.
For a bronchial infection: boil ammonia water, galbanum, honey and wine together, or else use a quarter-log of white goat milk.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Remedy: drip a liquid on cabbage stalks, stir with marjoram, and use dog feces mixed with balm, but do not eat the feces.
Remedy for stinging pain: turn over a stone called an arrow of Lilith and drink water; for uncovered water, drink undiluted wine.
Remedy for a pus-filled wound: drink a quarter-log of wine steeped in red ice plant.
Remedy for heart palpitations: barley loaves soaked in kamka, eaten and followed by diluted wine.
Rav Aḥa of Difti objects to Ravina: then such foods would make the heart palpitate even more.
Ravina replies that he meant the remedy for heaviness of the heart, not palpitations.
Alternative palpitation remedy: three wheat loaves soaked in honey, then undiluted wine.
Remedy for heart pain: mint, cumin and sesame in egg-bulk amounts, eaten together.
Remedy for intestinal pain: three hundred long peppers, a hundred a day with wine, which healed Rav Ashi's daughter.
Remedy for roundworm: wine steeped in laurel, and for white worm, cress soaked in water; be careful with the seed.
Chamomile: moist chamomile binds the bowels, dry chamomile in water relaxes them; a mnemonic is wet grass used to dam rivers.
Remedy for spleen illness: seven leeches dried and drunk with wine, or a goat spleen dried in an oven with an incantation.
Alternative spleen remedies: a goat spleen between bricks of a new house, or the hand of a man who died on Shabbat.
Remedy: roast a fish in a blacksmith's house and drink the water used to cool metal; a goat that drank it had no spleen.
Remedy: drink a large amount from a barrel of wine.
Rav Aḥa son of Rava objects to Rav Ashi: someone with a barrel of wine would not need a remedy from him.
Rav Ashi's reply: to stay healthy, one should eat bread in the morning, since it benefits the whole body.
Remedy for hemorrhoids: acacia, aloe, mercury and other ingredients in linen or cotton bags, or diluted beer.

Rava instead proposes a wording that begins with the negative outcome, then gives the death condition, then repeats the negative.
Rava's wording begins with the negative because a person does not hasten calamity upon himself.
Rava's full wording is: if I die it is a divorce, and if I do not die it is not, placing the affirmative first.
The affirmative must precede the negative, which is why this order is required.
Mishna: a husband conditions a divorce on his wife nursing his son or serving his father, with no time set; the required period is debated.
Mishna continues: if the condition is unfulfilled because the child or father dies, or the father refuses, the divorce is invalid.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules the divorce valid when an obstacle not caused by her prevents fulfilling the condition.
The Gemara asks whether she must fulfill the full stipulated period of service or nursing.
A baraita contradicts this: serving or nursing for a single day makes the divorce valid.
Rav Hisda resolves it: the baraita follows the Rabbis, and the mishna follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who allows giving the value of the item.
The Gemara challenges this: the mishna's attribution to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel implies the first clause is not his view, so the explanation fails.
Rava resolves it: the mishna is about an unspecified time, where the standard period applies, while the baraita states one day explicitly.
Rav Ashi resolves it differently: an unspecified condition counts as if one day was explicitly stated, so one day suffices.
The Gemara challenges Rav Ashi: why would the mishna specify two years or eighteen months if one day sufficed?
Rav Ashi replies that the mishna sets the period as one day within the two years, or eighteen months, to exclude later nursing.
An objection from the mishna's latter clause, where a father's refusal or the son's death makes the divorce invalid, challenges Rav Ashi's reading.

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: On Rava's reading, the mishna's first clause covers no stated period and the latter clause covers an explicit two-year period.
On Rav Ashi's reading, where one day suffices, the Gemara asks what distinguishes the first clause from the latter clause, and finds this difficult.
A baraita: a condition of serving his father or nursing his son for two years is void if not stated compoundly, per Rabbi Meir; the Rabbis disagree.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that no condition in Scripture is uncompounded, so every condition must be stated in both directions.
The Gemara explains Rabban Shimon's view as addressed to Rabbi Meir, whose compound verses teach only their own matter, not a general rule.
Others say he addresses the Rabbis, arguing that Scripture's conditions show a condition is valid only when it is compounded.
A contradicting baraita: if the father or son dies, the divorce is invalid, per Rabbi Meir, which seems to conflict with his other ruling.
The Rabbis hold the divorce valid despite non-fulfillment, since she could have offered to serve or nurse in place of the relative.
The Gemara notes the apparent conflict between two rulings of Rabbi Meir, and between two rulings of the Rabbis.
Both conflicts are resolved: Rabbi Meir's cases differ by whether the condition was compounded, and the Rabbis' cases differ by their views on hindrance.
The anonymous Rabbis in one baraita are identified as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who validates a divorce when an outside hindrance prevents the condition.
A baraita: a second condition said before witnesses does not cancel the first, so she may choose either condition and be divorced.
If the second condition is different and stated before witnesses, it cancels the first, and witnesses to the two conditions cannot combine.
The Gemara asks which clause of the baraita the non-combining of witnesses refers to.
It is needed to refer to the first clause, teaching that witnesses to different conditions cannot be combined to prove a divorce.
Mishna: a man going from Judea to Galilee who turns back at Antipatris within thirty days has his condition voided.
Likewise, a man going from Galilee to Judea who turns back at Kefar Otnai within thirty days has his condition voided.
Likewise, a man from Eretz Yisrael going overseas who turns back at Akko within thirty days has his condition voided.
If a husband leaves his wife's presence for thirty consecutive days, the divorce is valid, even with repeated trips, since they were not secluded.
The Gemara asks whether this means Antipatris was in the Galilee, given the mishna's wording.
A baraita places Antipatris in Judea and Kefar Otnai in the Galilee, with the area between treated as both, which contradicts that reading.

76b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abaye explains the mishna as two conditions, arriving in the Galilee or tarrying thirty days, and neither is met when he turns back at Antipatris.
The mishna continues with the Akko case: a divorce conditioned on not returning within thirty days from now.
The Gemara asks whether Akko is outside Eretz Yisrael, since the mishna's wording seems to imply that.
Rav Safra's report that Sages took leave in Akko, since leaving Eretz Yisrael is prohibited, indicates Akko lies within Eretz Yisrael.
Abaye explains the Akko case again: the two conditions are overseas arrival or tarrying thirty days, and neither occurred, so the condition is void.
The next mishna: a divorce conditioned on his leaving her presence for thirty consecutive days, while he keeps going and coming.
The Gemara asks whether he has not in fact passed from her presence, given his repeated coming and going.
Rav Huna explains that presence is a euphemism for intercourse, so the condition is about abstaining from relations for thirty days.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees: the condition is literal, so the divorce is valid once he is absent thirty consecutive days, not immediately.
A baraita follows Rabbi Yochanan: since he was not secluded with her, the divorce is not considered outdated and remains valid.
The Gemara asks whether there should be concern that he appeased her and secluded himself with her during that time.
Rabba bar Rav Huna cites Rav: the husband trusted her testimony, so if she says there was no seclusion, the divorce stands.
Some apply this same principle to the mishna on twelve months, where a death within the year still validates a divorce from now.
The Gemara asks whether there should be concern that he appeased her and was secluded with her in the twelve-month case.
Rabba bar Rav Huna again cites Rav: the husband stated she is believed, and he did not appease her, so the divorce is valid.
The Gemara concludes that whoever taught this about the mishna would apply it all the more to the baraita, but not vice versa.
Mishna: a divorce conditioned on not returning within twelve months is invalid if the husband dies within that year.
By contrast, a divorce stated as from now, if he does not return within twelve months, is valid if he dies within the year.
If he tells others to write and give the divorce if he does not return within twelve months, a delivery after twelve months is invalid.
Likewise, if the writing was done within the year but delivered after twelve months, the divorce is invalid.
Rabbi Yosei disagrees and holds that such a divorce is valid, since the husband set only the time of delivery.
If the husband dies between writing and delivery, the divorce is valid only if delivered before his death, and uncertainty arises if the order is unknown.
A baraita reports that the Sages permitted the woman to remarry without halitza, treating the divorce as valid.
The Gemara asks who the Sages in this baraita are.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, identifies them as the court that permitted gentile oil, holding with Rabbi Yosei that a document's date shows when it takes effect.
Rabbi Yochanan reports that Rabbi Yehuda Nesia taught this view, but his colleagues did not concede to his opinion.
Rabbi Elazar asks an elder of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's court whether the permission was granted immediately or only after twelve months.
The Gemara asks the same dilemma about the mishna's case: is the divorce effective immediately at death, or only after twelve months?
The Gemara answers yes, the dilemma applies to the mishna too, and Rabbi Elazar asked because that elder witnessed the actual incident.
Abaye says everyone agrees that if the husband ties the divorce to the sun emerging from its sheath, the divorce takes effect at that time.

77a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the husband says the divorce takes effect when the sun emerges, and dies at night before that, the divorce is after death and invalid.
Rav Huna cites Rav: a conditional wording is equivalent to a wording stating the divorce takes effect from now, which supports the earlier reading.
The tanna'im dispute only the case of the sun-emerges wording: one view follows Rabbi Yosei's dating rule, the other does not.
The mishna: a divorce to be written and given if he does not return within twelve months is invalid if delivered after that period, with Rabbi Yosei disagreeing.
Rav Yeimar asks Rav Ashi whether Rabbi Yosei generally holds a conditional divorce valid even if the condition is unfulfilled.
Rav Ashi replies that the wording differs: stating the instruction as from now is a different case, and the Rabbis do not distinguish such minor wording.
A baraita sets timing for after-clauses: after a week, year, month, or Sabbatical cycle means a further full unit beyond it.
Rabbi Asi's ruling on a week: Sunday to Tuesday are considered after Shabbat, while Wednesday to Friday are considered before Shabbat.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view that a divorce conditioned on not returning after the festival takes effect thirty days later is not accepted as halakha.
Mishna: a divorce thrown into her house or courtyard is valid if she is inside, invalid if thrown into his, and valid if thrown into her lap or basket.
The Gemara asks from where the rules of the mishna's halakha about throwing a divorce are derived.
A baraita derives the rule from the verse 'and gives it in her hand', read with 'and gives' to include any manner of delivery.
A parallel baraita derives the rule on theft from 'found in his hand', read to include an item found in his domain.
Both derivations are needed: a divorce might be viewed as effective even against her will, while a thief's liability might be narrowed by analogy.
The Gemara asks how a wife can own a courtyard, given that what a wife acquires belongs to her husband.
Rabbi Elazar says the mishna means the husband wrote that he has no involvement in her property, relinquishing his rights.
The Gemara asks what effect such a writing has, since a baraita holds that similar disclaimers in partnership do not withdraw rights.
The school of Rabbi Yannai says the case is when she is still betrothed, so he has not yet gained rights, consistent with Rav Kahana and Rava.

77b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava says that one may decline a rabbinic ordinance enacted for one's benefit, and in such a case we listen to the person who declines it.
The Gemara asks what case Rava means by 'such as this' and which earlier ruling he is referring to.
Rav Huna cites Rav: a wife may waive maintenance in exchange for her work, so an ordinance for her benefit can be declined.
Rava resolves the courtyard question directly: her hand and the divorce enter her possession together, so the courtyard can be treated the same way.
Ravina asks why Rava would find it difficult to accept that the divorce takes effect when placed in her hand.
Rav Ashi replies that the same difficulty arises for a slave's manumission, so the bill and the hand must enter together, applying also to the courtyard.
A dying man wrote a divorce for his wife on Shabbat eve but could not deliver it, and people came before Rava about the situation.
Rava instructs them to transfer to her the place where the bill rests, so she can take possession by closing and opening the door.
A Bava Batra mishna is cited: locking, fencing, or breaching a place, of any size, constitutes a valid act of acquiring possession.
Rav Ilish objects to Rava that a wife's acquisitions belong to her husband, so the place cannot be acquired for her.
Rava is vindicated: the woman was betrothed, not married, and a betrothed woman's acquisitions are not her husband's, so the courtyard works.
The Gemara asks why Rava needed to state this principle again, since he had already said it earlier.
The mishna says a divorce thrown while she is in her house is valid; Ulla and Rabbi Oshaya differ on whether her house and courtyard may be in separate cities.
The Gemara objects that the mishna itself says she is in her house and courtyard, which would require both to be in one place.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is whether the courtyard works as an extension of her hand or as an agent, which affects its location requirement.
The Gemara rejects that: everyone agrees the courtyard is an extension of her hand, and they differ only on how close it must be.
Rabbi Oshaya's view is explained: the courtyard must be consciously secured by her, which excludes one she does not control.
A man threw a divorce to his wife in a courtyard and it fell on a board, and Rav Yosef rules by the board's size, four by four cubits.
The Gemara asks which case this refers to, since if the board is hers or his, the four-cubit size seems to make no difference.
The case is one where he lent her the courtyard, and people lend one place but not two, so a separate board area is not covered.
The halakha applies only if the board is not ten handbreadths higher than the courtyard, since a higher board is a separate domain regardless of size.
The Gemara adds the qualification that the ruling applies only where the board has no area of its own, which is cut off at the end.

78a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The modifier shows the board has its own name, so even if it is low and small it counts as a separate domain and the divorce is invalid.
Mishna: a bill thrown while she is in his house is invalid, even on the bed; Rava limits this to his bed, so if it is her bed she is divorced.
A baraita with Rabbi Eliezer's view: throwing the bill when she is on his bed is invalid, on her bed valid.
The Gemara asks whether a bill thrown onto her bed takes effect, given that the bed may be treated like a buyer's vessels in the seller's domain.
The distinction is needed when the bed is ten handbreadths high, and its legs' location is ignored because people are not particular about such a small spot.
Mishna: a bill thrown into her lap or basket takes effect even while she is in her husband's house.
The Gemara asks why this is valid, since the basket may be the buyer's vessel in the seller's domain.
Several explanations are offered: the basket hangs from her body, is tied to her, lies between her thighs, or belongs to a basket seller's courtyard.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that the place of her lap and basket is hers, so no further explanation is needed.
Rava explains Rabbi Yochanan's view: a husband is not particular about his wife's lap or basket, so he effectively transfers that place to her.
A baraita: a bill thrown into her lap, basket, or anything like her basket makes her divorced.
The Gemara asks what the words 'anything like her basket' are meant to include.
They include a basket in which she carries dates, since the husband is not particular about its place either.
Mishna: if he gives her a document that turns out to be a bill of divorce, it is invalid until he says it is her bill of divorce.
The same applies if he places the bill in her hand while she sleeps and she reads it after waking, until he declares it her bill.
The Gemara asks what effect the declaration has if the bill was left on the ground behind him, since it is not properly given.
Rava holds that saying take your bill from where it lies on the ground is no divorce, since she must receive it from him.
The Gemara suggests the bill was tucked in his belt and she pulled it out, so she received it from him.
The Gemara objects that a pulled-out bill does not fulfill the requirement that he give it into her hand.
The case is one where he bent his waist toward her, so her pulling it out amounts to him giving it to her.
A baraita: a bill handed over as a document or pulled from behind him is valid only once he declares it, per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi; Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar requires redelivery.
The baraita's second case repeats the dispute for a bill placed in her hand while she sleeps, with the same two positions.
Both cases must be stated, since one could otherwise think the disagreement applies only to one of them.
Rava holds that a bill placed in the hand of a slave who guards his sleeping master is valid, since the slave is like her courtyard.
The Gemara asks why a sleeping slave's courtyard works when a mobile courtyard does not acquire for its owner.
Rava's principle is that a person who does not acquire while moving does not acquire while still, and the ruling applies only where the slave is bound.
Mishna: a bill thrown to a woman standing in the public domain takes effect if it lands closer to her, and not if closer to him, with the same rule for betrothal.
The same rule applies to a debt payment thrown to a creditor, with the outcome depending on which party the money lands closer to.
Rav explains closer as within four cubits of her or of him, and the Gemara clarifies the same for the debt case.
The Gemara asks what counts as midway between the two parties.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says midway means both stood within the same four cubits.
The Gemara asks which party entered the four cubits first, and whether simultaneous arrival can be precisely established.
Rav Kahana says the case is eight cubits exactly, with his four cubits adjacent to her four cubits, so precision is possible.

78b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The bill of divorce extends from his four cubits into her four cubits, so part of it is in each domain and the outcome is uncertain.
The Gemara asks whether the bill is still attached to him, since part of it lies within his four cubits.
Rabba and Rav Yosef both explain that the case involves two groups of witnesses, so balanced refers to their differing accounts, not distance.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that closer to her means actually closer, even if a hundred cubits away, and likewise for him.
The Gemara asks what the balanced case is under Rabbi Yochanan's reading of the mishna.
Rav Shemen bar Abba reports Rabbi Yochanan's test: whoever can guard the bill is closer to that party, and if both or neither can, it is balanced.
Rabbi Yochanan is amazed that Babylonian scholars reached the same explanation, which the Rabbis had transmitted in the name of Rabbi Yonatan.
A baraita: if a dog takes a bill that was closer to her before it reached her hand, she is not divorced, per Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara asks why she is not divorced, since it was already closer to her, and whether she must keep guarding it.
The baraita means that a dog could be guarded by him but not by her, so the bill is in his domain and she is not divorced.
Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda that closer to her means she must be able to bend and take it, and no action should permit remarriage before it reaches her hand.
Rav Mordekhai relates a case where a bill closer to the woman was lost, so the Sages required halitza before she could remarry.
Mishna: the same rules apply to betrothal; Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, says these rules apply only to divorce, not other matters.
Rabbi Abba objects to Rabbi Asi from the mishna's explicit statement that the same rules apply to betrothal.
Rabbi Abba answers that betrothal differs, since the verse uses the same wording for betrothal as for divorce, so only that link is valid.
Another objection comes from a baraita applying the same divorce rules to debt payments, which suggests debt follows divorce law.
The case is one where the creditor says throw the payment to me so that you are released, and the stipulation matters only if it names the divorce procedure.
The Gemara asks why the stipulation needs stating if the creditor explicitly named the divorce procedure, and why it is taught.
Rav Hisda holds that if the husband can still pull the bill from her hand by a string, she is not divorced, and otherwise she is.
The reason is that severance is required, and here it is lacking because the husband still holds the bill.
Rav Yehuda holds that if her hand slopes so the bill cannot stay and falls out, she is not divorced, even though it reached her hand.
The Gemara asks why, since a fallen bill lands within her four cubits, Rav Yehuda's case is not simply within her domain.
The Gemara asks why she is not divorced when the bill was in her airspace, and proposes resolving Rabbi Elazar's dilemma on airspace from this case.
The Gemara rejects that inference: the case may be a woman standing at a riverbank, where the bill is destined to fall and be lost.

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a bill thrown from a roof to a woman below, or from below to a woman on the roof, takes effect once it reaches the roof's airspace or leaves its area.
The Gemara asks: isn't the roof's airspace unsecured, since wind can carry the bill away, so it should not count as her domain?
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says the roof has a parapet, so it is secured, and Ulla bar Menashya adds that a bill within three handbreadths of the roof counts as on it.
The mishna's second case continues: he is above on the roof and she is below.
The Gemara asks again whether the airspace of the courtyard is unsecured, since wind can blow the bill out.
Shmuel, Rabbi Elazar and Ulla each say the case is where the lower partitions extend beyond the upper ones, so the bill surely lands in the courtyard.
Rabbi Abba asks Ulla whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who treats an object in airspace as resting.
Ulla replies that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi only regarding Shabbat, whereas here the bill is secured and so the divorce takes effect.
The Gemara asks why the bill is considered secured if it is still being guarded in the air.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Yochanan, gives the same explanation of partitions extending beyond each other.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view that airspace counts as resting.
Rabbi Asi replies the same way: the Rabbis disagree with that view only for Shabbat, while in divorce the bill is secured.
Rav Nachman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, limits the ruling on erasure: a bill erased on descent counts, but not one erased while ascending.
Likewise, if the bill was burned before it was thrown, she is not divorced, since it was already destined for burning.
Rav Hisda holds that domains are divided with regard to bills of divorce, so separate areas within one domain count as separate domains.
Rami bar Hama asks Rava where the Elder, meaning Rav Hisda, derives this principle.
Rava answers that the mishna's roof case, in which she is divorced once the bill reaches the roof's airspace, shows the principle.
The Gemara asks which case the mishna addresses: her roof with her courtyard, his roof with his courtyard, or a mixed case.
Obviously the case is her roof and his courtyard, so the latter clause must be considered.
The latter clause is quoted: if he is above and she is below, she is divorced once the bill leaves the roof's area, even if erased or burned.
Rava asks why she is divorced in the case of her roof and his courtyard, since the bill has not left his domain.
Rather, it must be his roof and her courtyard; the mishna lent her a place, and people lend one place but not two.
Rami bar Hama objects that the two clauses may describe two different cases, so the mishna is not proof for Rav Hisda's principle.
Rava states three distinctions between divorce and Shabbat; the first is that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's airspace rule applies only to Shabbat.
Here, in divorce, the bill is secured while within the airspace of partitions, so the Rabbis agree she is divorced.
The Gemara asks why the bill is considered secured when it is not being guarded.
The second distinction: Rav Hisda's rule that an object landing on a reed in a private domain is liable applies only to Shabbat, not to divorce.
The Gemara asks why the bill is secured when it is on the reed and not being guarded.

79b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel's rule: one may not stand on his roof to collect rain from a neighbor's roof on Shabbat, since separate residences form separate domains above and below.
Rava limits this to Shabbat: for divorce, a husband is particular only about one place, so an adjacent roof he owns still counts as her domain.
Abaye's case: an inner courtyard is hers within his outer courtyard, and a bill reaching the air above the outer partitions divorces her.
The reason is that the outer partitions secure the inner courtyard, so the bill is treated as hers once it reaches that airspace.
The Gemara contrasts baskets: with one basket inside another, a bill reaching the inner basket's airspace does not divorce her unless it lands in it.
The reason is that the bill had not yet come to rest in the basket, and the outer basket's walls do not secure the inner one.
The Gemara asks what difference it makes once the bill rests in the basket, since her basket lies within his domain like a buyer's vessels.
The case is a basket with no bottom, so the inner basket rests on the ground outside his and the bill in it divorces her.
Mishna: Beit Shammai allow divorcing with an outdated bill, while Beit Hillel forbid it; an outdated bill is one written before seclusion with her.
The Gemara asks what the point of disagreement between these two schools is.
Beit Shammai do not apply the decree that a bill is invalid, since the decree is that people would think she conceived before the divorce, while Beit Hillel do.
Shmuel holds that a woman who remarried on an outdated bill need not leave her second husband, and such a bill may be used ab initio.
Mishna: a bill dated by an illegitimate kingdom's calendar or by the Temple era, or placed in the wrong east or west, is invalid.
Mishna continues: she loses her marriage contract, profits, sustenance and claims, and her children from either marriage are mamzerim.
The mishna concludes: an Israelite woman who married both men is disqualified from marrying a priest, as a zonah.

80a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Through these two marriages a Levite's daughter loses her tithe rights and a priest's daughter loses her teruma rights, even if she returns to her father's house.
Neither set of heirs inherits her marriage contract, and the brothers of each husband perform halitza, not levirate marriage, since she was betrothed to the second.
If the bill misnames a husband, a wife, or a city, and she remarries on it, she must leave both men and the same penalties apply.
When the widow is forbidden to the brother, the rival wives of the deceased are permitted to marry without levirate marriage or halitza.
If the forbidden widow proves an ailonit, her marriage was never valid, so the rival wives must leave both men and the same penalties apply.
Likewise for one who married his yevama: if her rival wife remarried and the yevama proves an ailonit, the rival must leave both men.
A scribe erred, giving the bill to the wife and the receipt to the husband, so the two exchanged documents and no divorce occurred.
If later the bill and receipt are found in the wrong hands, and she remarried, she must leave both men and the same penalties apply.
Rabbi Elazar: if the bill is still in the husband's possession immediately, it is invalid, but if after time, it is valid, since the first husband cannot undo the second's right.
The Gemara asks what is meant by a kingdom that is not legitimate.
It refers to the Roman Empire, dated in a land where Rome did not rule, and it is so called because Romans had no script or language of their own.
Ulla explains the Sages instituted dating by the local kingdom to maintain peaceful relations with the government.
The Gemara asks whether the Sages would be so strict as to make a woman leave her husband and her children mamzerim, for the sake of peace.
Yes: Rabbi Meir holds that any deviation from the formula invalidates the bill, so a remarriage makes the offspring mamzerim.
The mishna states that dating by the Greek Empire invalidates a bill of divorce.
The Gemara explains why each kingdom and the Temple dating must be stated, since each raises a different concern about government sensitivity.
Mishna: if he was in the east and wrote the location as the west, the bill is invalid.
The Gemara asks who the mishna is about, since a changed location would be the same as the earlier case of changed names.
It refers to a scribe who wrote the wrong location: Rav and Rav Huna told their scribes to write the actual place where the document was written.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, begins a further statement, which is cut off at the end.

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir is strict about dating by the kingdom, but the Rabbis hold a bill dated by a local guardsman is still valid, so she is divorced.
A bill was dated by the governor of Bascar's years, and Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda brought the dilemma to Rabba.
Rabba replies that even Rabbi Meir concedes, since the governor is an official of that kingdom, so the ruler does not object.
The Gemara asks how this case differs from the guardsman in the city.
Naming a minor guardsman demeans the kingdom, while naming a senior governor flatters it, so the two cases differ.
Rav Huna, citing Rav, says the mishna follows Rabbi Meir, who holds such a child a mamzer, while the Rabbis hold the lineage unflawed.
Rav Ashi cites the mishna on changed names and cities, which renders the woman's remarriage penalized, as support.
The Gemara asks which tanna teaches that halakha, and whether it is Rabbi Meir's view.
The halakha must be the Rabbis' view, since Rabbi Meir would have combined the two cases; the mishna switches to the Rabbis here.
Mishna: rival wives of a forbidden widow who married, once the widow is shown to be an ailonit, are subject to the same penalties.
The Gemara suggests this refutes Rav Hamnuna, who holds that a yevama who engaged in licentious intercourse is forbidden to her yavam.
No refutation: the mishna speaks of marriage as a euphemism, and the same holds for licentious intercourse.
Some say the exchange ran differently: the mishna implies the rule for marriage applies equally to licentious intercourse.
The Gemara suggests the mishna supports Rav Hamnuna, who holds the yevama who sinned is forbidden to her yavam.
No: the prohibition applies only where she married, since she could be confused with a woman whose husband went overseas and who remarried.
Mishna: one who married his yevama, and her rival then married another man, and the yevama is shown to be an ailonit, faces penalties.
This halakha must be taught separately, because in the earlier case levirate marriage was never performed, while here it was, so the rival is not blamed.
Mishna: a scribe who erred, giving the bill to the woman and the receipt to the husband, produces no valid divorce if the bill is with him immediately.
Rabbi Eliezer's position: if the bill is in the husband's possession after some time, the divorce is presumed valid and returned later.
The Gemara asks what counts as immediately and what counts as after some time.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: while the parties are still seated and engaged in the matter, it is immediate; once they rise and finish, it is after some time.
Rav Adda bar Ahava: if she was not yet married to someone else, it counts as immediate, since the matter can be corrected; if married, it counts as after some time.
The mishna states that the first husband cannot eliminate the second husband's right.
The Gemara asks how the mention of a second husband fits Rav Adda bar Ahava's view.
The Gemara asks what the reference to a second husband means on Shmuel's view, where no second husband exists.

81a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara clarifies that the first husband cannot eliminate the right of a suitor who wishes to marry her, not a second husband already married.
